courseMetadata.title: Auth & Security Fundamentals
courseMetadata.description: Build authentication you can defend. You will implement session- and token-based auth, enforce authorization at the object level, configure CORS without over-permissioning, and then **attack your own application** to find out which of your defences actually work. For senior developers who already build APIs.

prerequisites.description: Experience building HTTP APIs — routing, middleware, request/response handling.
Basic familiarity with HTTP headers and cookies: what `Set-Cookie` does, what a request header is.
Comfortable reading JavaScript. Two exercises use Python and SQL, both explained inline.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: The bearer-credential idea is introduced in section 1, exploited in section 2 (CSRF rides the cookie) and dissolved in section 3 (XSS bypasses HttpOnly). Injecting siblings forces the learner to meet it in a changed frame rather than in the section that taught it.
Trust-boundary thinking runs from 'is this login leaking existence' through 'is this record theirs' to 'did this data cross into an interpreter'. Same question, three disguises.

probeQuestions.prompt: You inherit a service that stores passwords as `sha256(salt + password)`, with a unique 16-byte random salt per user. An attacker steals the database. What is the situation?
options: Adequate — the per-user salt defeats precomputation, which is the main threat.
The salt defeats precomputation, but SHA-256's speed still allows fast offline brute-forcing of each row individually.
Insecure because the salt sits in plaintext beside the hash; salts belong in a secrets manager.
Secure as long as the salt is at least 32 bytes and the database is encrypted at rest.

optionFeedback.feedback: Precomputation is only one of two attacks. Each row can still be brute-forced on its own at GPU speed, because the hash is fast by design.
Exactly right, and the distinction matters: salting and slowness fix two different attacks, and this system has only fixed one of them.
Salts are not secrets and never were — they must be readable to verify a login at all. Their job is to stop precomputation and cross-user reuse.
Neither salt length nor encryption at rest addresses speed, and an attacker holding a database dump has decrypted data by definition.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: Passwords stored as fast-hash plus per-user salt: which attack is defeated, and which is still wide open?

routingRules.action: mark credential-handling as partially known; keep the worked example but skip the remedial callout
surface the two-attacks worked example early in exp-identity-mechanics

probeQuestions.prompt: A user clicks **Log out**. Your handler calls `res.clearCookie("sid")` and returns 200. Someone copied that session identifier from a proxy log an hour ago. What can they do now?
options: Nothing — the cookie was deleted, so the session is gone.
Nothing, provided the cookie was set with HttpOnly and Secure.
Everything the user could do — the server-side session was never deleted, and their copy still authenticates.
Only read operations; write operations would need a fresh login.

optionFeedback.feedback: Clearing the cookie removes one copy of a bearer credential from one browser. The server's session record is untouched.
Those attributes govern how the cookie is stored and transmitted. Neither has any bearing on whether the server still considers the session valid.
Correct — and this is why logout must be a server-side delete. The cookie clear is tidying up afterwards, not the operation itself.
The server cannot tell the two holders apart at all; there is no mechanism here that would restrict one to reads.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: Logout clears the cookie and nothing else. What is still true for someone holding a copy of that identifier?

options: Nothing — requireLogin ensures only authenticated customers reach the handler.
Nothing, as long as the front-end only ever links to invoices belonging to the current customer.
Read any invoice in the system by changing the id in the URL.
Read invoices only if they can guess the database's internal numbering scheme.

optionFeedback.feedback: requireLogin is authentication — it establishes who is calling. It has no opinion about which records that person may read.
The UI is a rendering of a decision, running on a machine the attacker controls. The endpoint is the real interface and accepts any id you send it.
Correct. This is IDOR/BOLA — a direct object reference with no check that the caller may follow it — and it is the most-reported API vulnerability in the field.
Unguessable identifiers are obscurity, not a check: ids leak through referrers, logs, exports and shared links, and any leaked id grants full access.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: A handler loads a record by a caller-supplied id after requireLogin and returns it. Name the vulnerability class.

probeQuestions.prompt: Your API allows only `https://app.example.com`. A page on `https://evil.test` sends a cross-origin `POST` with a form-encoded body and `credentials: "include"`. The browser console shows a CORS error. What happened **on your server**?
options: Nothing — the browser blocked the request before it left.
The request arrived and the handler ran; only the response was withheld from the calling page.
The request arrived but without cookies, so it ran unauthenticated.
The server rejected it because the Origin header was not in the allowlist.

optionFeedback.feedback: That is true of preflighted requests only. This one is a simple request: it was sent, and whatever it changed is changed.
Correct — and this is precisely why CORS is not a defence for state-changing endpoints. It governs reading, not doing.
This conflates CORS with SameSite. Whether cookies attach is decided by the cookie's own attributes, not by your CORS configuration.
Unless you wrote an explicit server-side Origin check, your server does not reject anything here — it simply omits a response header.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: A CORS error appears in the console after a cross-origin POST. What already happened on the server?

options: The claims may be stale if the user's role changed after the token was issued.
The payload is readable by the client, so the role is exposed.
No signature is verified, so anyone can mint a token claiming to be an admin.
The token could be replayed from another service that shares the signing key.

optionFeedback.feedback: Real and worth fixing, but far less severe: staleness requires a legitimately issued token, while the option below requires nothing at all.
Also true and inherent to JWTs — the payload is encoded, not encrypted — but disclosure is not the severe problem here.
Correct. `decode` parses without verifying, so every claim it returns is attacker-supplied and this check is trivially forgeable.
A genuine audience-confusion risk, but it presupposes that verification happens at all — and here it does not.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: Code reads a role claim straight from `jwt.decode(token)`. What is the worst consequence?

probeQuestions.prompt: A handler needs to let users choose the sort column: `ORDER BY ${req.query.sort}`. Which fix is correct?
options: Escape the value with the driver's string-escaping function, then interpolate it.
Pass it as a bound parameter: ORDER BY ?.
Map the input through an allowlist of permitted column names and reject anything unmatched.
Strip all non-alphanumeric characters from the input, then interpolate.

optionFeedback.feedback: Escaping applies to string literals. A column name is an identifier, so escaping either breaks the query or leaves it injectable.
Reasonable instinct, wrong mechanism: placeholders bind values, so `ORDER BY ?` sorts by a constant and silently does nothing useful.
Correct. The user's input selects a key; the column name comes from your map, so the interpolated text never originates with the user.
Reduces the surface without closing it, and it is the escaping-instead-of-separating pattern wearing a different hat.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: A user picks the SQL sort column. Parameterization cannot bind it. What is the correct technique?

probeQuestions.prompt: An attacker achieves stored XSS on a site whose session cookies are `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict`, and which uses per-request CSRF tokens. In your own words, describe what the attacker can and cannot do, and say which of those three protections still helps.
scoringCriteria: Says the attacker **cannot read** the cookie value — HttpOnly genuinely blocks exfiltration of the identifier.
Says the attacker **can still act** as the user, because the browser attaches the cookie to requests the injected script makes.
Notes that `SameSite` does not apply, because script running in your origin makes same-site requests.
Notes that CSRF tokens are readable from the DOM by that same script.
Reaches the conclusion that this is full compromise within the origin, not a defaced page.
probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: Stored XSS on a site with HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict and CSRF tokens: what survives, and what does not?

probeQuestions.prompt: You try a CSRF attack against your own staging app. The forged request fails. Describe exactly what you would do next before writing "CSRF: not exploitable" in an audit document — and explain why that step is not optional.
scoringCriteria: Proposes disabling the control believed responsible and re-running the attack to confirm it then succeeds.
Explains that a failure can be incidental — a malformed payload, a framework default, a stripped header, a dev-mode difference.
Notes that without this step you have not identified **which** control did the work, so you cannot know what a future refactor will break.
Mentions re-enabling the control and recording both results.
probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: Before recording "attack failed" in an audit, what must you do, and why?

competencies.title: Secure credential storage and verification
competencies.description: Store and verify user secrets with memory-hard hashing, per-user salts, constant-time comparison, and login paths that leak nothing about which accounts exist.

desiredOutcomes.description: Store passwords so that a stolen database is not a list of passwords.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Chooses a memory-hard function with a justified work factor and per-user salts; can explain which attack each element defeats.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build a login path whose message, status code and duration are identical whether or not the account exists.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names all three leak channels unprompted and equalises all three, including the dummy-hash timing fix.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: SHA-256 with a salt is fine for storing passwords.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The salt fixes precomputation only. SHA-256 is engineered to be fast — billions of guesses per second on a GPU — so every row can still be brute-forced individually. A password hash must be deliberately slow and memory-hard; speed is the vulnerability.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the worked example that separates the two attacks: show that salting defeats rainbow tables while leaving per-row brute force untouched, then compare a fast hash's guess rate against a tuned bcrypt/Argon2 work factor.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Salts have to be kept secret, ideally in a secrets manager.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Salts are stored in plaintext next to the hash and must be readable to verify a login at all. Their job is to destroy precomputation and cross-user reuse, not to hide anything. Treating them as secrets pushes teams toward a single global value, which reintroduces exactly the attack salts exist to stop.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner trace the verification path and identify the step that becomes impossible if the salt is unavailable; then contrast per-user salt with a single global pepper.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: As long as both failures return the same error message, attackers cannot tell which emails have accounts.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Matching text closes one channel of three. The status code is machine-readable, and the response duration differs because the 'no such user' path skips the expensive hash entirely. A timing oracle is as scriptable as a message.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run the 50-logins timing measurement from the practical activity and compare medians; then apply the dummy-hash fix and measure again.

competencies.title: Server-side sessions and cookie transport
competencies.description: Issue, transport, rotate and revoke opaque session identifiers, and choose cookie attributes deliberately rather than by copying a snippet.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement a session lifecycle where logout actually ends the session and login rotates the identifier.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Logout deletes server-side state; a pre-login identifier stops resolving after authentication.

desiredOutcomes.description: Justify each cookie attribute by naming what breaks without it.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Distinguishes what HttpOnly and SameSite each do and do not prevent, and refuses a widened Domain with a reason.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Clearing the cookie in the browser logs the user out.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The cookie is one copy of a bearer credential, not the session. Deleting it client-side leaves the server-side session valid, so any copy an attacker took still authenticates. Logout is a server-side delete; clearing the cookie is tidying up afterwards.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Replay the predict-run snippet where the client variable is nulled and the server map is untouched, then have the learner curl a copied identifier after logging out.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The session cookie is encrypted, so its contents are safe.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Frameworks typically sign cookies, which proves the server issued the value and that nobody altered it — but signing is not encryption and the value stays readable. With an opaque identifier this is beside the point anyway: the exposure is not the contents, it is possession.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Contrast signing with encryption directly, then point out that an opaque identifier has nothing to read — theft, not disclosure, is the threat.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: SameSite=Lax makes CSRF impossible.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Lax closes the common case and is worth having, but three gaps remain: state-changing endpoints reachable by GET still receive the cookie on top-level navigation; subdomains are same-site, so a compromised sibling host is not cross-site at all; and non-browser clients ignore the mechanism entirely.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Work the cookie-attachment predictor exercise until the learner can state both bypassing contexts from memory, then layer a session-bound token on top.

competencies.title: Token-based authentication and JWT validation
competencies.description: Issue and validate signed tokens, verify algorithm, signature, expiry and audience in the right order, and design refresh and revocation knowing what statelessness costs.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write a validator that fails closed against unsigned, tampered, expired and wrong-audience tokens.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Verifies the signature before reading any claim and takes the algorithm from configuration, never from the token.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a revocation strategy and state plainly what statelessness was traded away to get it.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Proposes short access tokens plus rotating server-side refresh tokens, and acknowledges that a hard revocation deadline forces real server state.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A JWT is secure because it is signed — its contents cannot be read.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Signing gives integrity and origin: nobody altered it and it came from a key holder. It gives nothing on confidentiality — the payload is base64url, readable by anyone holding the token — and nothing on freshness, so a token minted before an account was suspended stays valid until it expires.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Decode a token payload in front of the learner with no key at all, then ask what would still be true if the user had been banned one minute after issuance.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Decoding a token and reading its claims is validating it.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A decode parses without checking the signature, so any claim it returns is attacker-supplied. Worse, taking the algorithm from the token's own header lets an attacker choose how their token is checked: `alg: none` accepts unsigned tokens, and downgrading RS256 to HS256 lets them sign with your public key as the shared secret.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run the validator challenge with the alg-from-token variant and watch the forged admin token pass; then move the algorithm into configuration and watch it fail.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Tokens are stateless, so they are strictly better than sessions.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Statelessness is a performance property with a security cost. Logout, ban, role change and password reset all require the server to change its mind about a credential it already issued — precisely what statelessness forbids. Every real deployment reintroduces state somewhere; the design question is how much and where.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give a hard revocation deadline (60 seconds) and have the learner discover that meeting it requires a denylist lookup — then name the property they gave up.

competencies.title: Authorization and role-based access control
competencies.description: Separate authentication from authorization and enforce role and ownership rules server-side, at the layer that can actually see the record.

desiredOutcomes.description: Enforce object-level ownership checks so changing an identifier in a URL reaches nothing new.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Writes a default-deny policy function called after the record loads, with negative cases outnumbering positive ones in its tests.

desiredOutcomes.description: Place each authorization check at the layer that has the information it needs.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Explains why role checks suit middleware and ownership checks cannot, without resorting to the UI as an enforcement argument.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: They are logged in and the UI hides the button, so they cannot do it.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The UI is a rendering of a decision, made on a machine the attacker controls. The endpoint is the actual interface, and it is directly callable with any parameters forever. Hidden controls change what is convenient, never what is possible.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner curl the endpoint whose button their own UI hides, with a valid low-privilege session, and capture the successful response.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Checking the user's role is enough authorization.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A role answers 'what kind of user', never 'whose record'. Almost every breach in this class is an ownership failure by a user whose role was entirely correct — a real teacher reading another class's submissions. Both checks are required and neither substitutes for the other.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Walk the policy matrix where two users share a role and differ only in assignment, and show the role check approving both.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: All authorization belongs in route middleware.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Route middleware runs before the record is loaded, so it has nothing to compare the user against. Forcing object-level rules into it produces either no check at all or a second query that silently drifts out of sync with the handler's own.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Trace the request lifecycle and mark the exact point at which the record first exists; place the ownership check after it.

competencies.title: CORS and the same-origin boundary
competencies.description: Explain what the same-origin policy actually protects, and configure cross-origin access to the minimum an application genuinely needs.

desiredOutcomes.description: Configure CORS with an exact-match allowlist and no reflected origins.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Uses exact string matching, enumerates methods and headers, adds Vary: Origin, and gates localhost on non-production.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: CORS is a security feature that protects my API.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: CORS is a relaxation mechanism, not a restriction. It is enforced by browsers on responses, so it protects users' browsers from a hostile page reading cross-origin data. curl, a script, a mobile app or any server ignores it completely. If your API's safety depends on CORS, your API has no safety.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner call their own CORS-restricted endpoint with curl and observe a normal successful response.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Setting Access-Control-Allow-Origin to * is a quick fix, and reflecting the Origin header is the safe version of it.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The wildcard cannot be combined with credentials, so it never fixes an authenticated API — and the reflection people reach for next is strictly worse: it grants every origin on the internet credentialed read access. The wildcard was at least honest about being open.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run the allowlist-versus-reflection example and read the emitted header aloud with an attacker origin in it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A CORS error in the console means the request was blocked.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: For a simple request the browser sent it, your server executed it, the row was written and the email went out — only the response was withheld from the calling page. Just preflighted requests are genuinely stopped before arrival. The rejection is about reading, not about doing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Send a cross-origin POST from a scratch page against a restrictive CORS config, then check the database for the write.

competencies.title: Cross-site request forgery and ambient authority
competencies.description: Recognise the confused-deputy pattern created by automatically attached credentials, and layer defences while naming what each layer misses.

desiredOutcomes.description: Defend state-changing endpoints in layers and state the residual risk of each.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Combines SameSite, a session-bound token and an Origin check, and identifies XSS as the condition under which all three fail at once.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: CSRF is irrelevant for APIs that use an Authorization: Bearer header.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: True only while credentials are never ambient. The moment any path falls back to cookies — a refresh-token cookie, a legacy endpoint, a 'remember me' flow, a server-rendered admin page — ambient authority returns and so does CSRF. Audit for cookie-carrying paths instead of assuming the header-only design holds everywhere.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner inventory every path in their app that authenticates via a cookie rather than an explicit header.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Checking the Referer header is a sufficient CSRF defence.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Referer can be stripped or absent — privacy settings, noreferrer, protocol transitions — which forces a choice between rejecting legitimate users and allowing empty values, and 'allow if absent' is trivially exploitable. Origin is more reliable but still belongs as one layer, never the sole control.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Log Origin and Referer presence across real traffic for a day before proposing either as a control.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: CSRF tokens also protect against XSS.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The relationship runs the other way and only one way. Script executing in your origin can simply read the token out of the DOM and include it, so XSS defeats every CSRF defence at once. They address different problems and one of them dominates the other.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Read the token from the DOM in the browser console to demonstrate the bypass, then re-rank the two risks.

competencies.title: Cross-site scripting and output encoding
competencies.description: Distinguish stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS, encode for the sink's context, and treat script injection as total compromise of the origin.

desiredOutcomes.description: Apply the right encoding for each output context and explain why input sanitisation is the wrong layer.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Uses different encoders for HTML body, attribute and URL contexts, and gives both reasons output encoding wins.

desiredOutcomes.description: Rank XSS impact correctly against the defences built earlier in the course.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: States that HttpOnly, SameSite and CSRF tokens are all bypassed, and why each fails.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Escaping < and > when input arrives handles XSS.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That covers one context partially. Inside a quoted attribute a lone double quote closes the attribute and starts new ones — an event handler needs no angle brackets at all. And in an href, `javascript:` contains no HTML metacharacters whatsoever. Dangerous characters are a property of the context, not of the value.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run the attribute-breakout snippet where angle-bracket escaping is applied and the payload still executes.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: My framework auto-escapes, so I am safe from XSS.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Auto-escaping covers text interpolation and eliminates most XSS, which is a genuine win. It stops at raw-HTML props like dangerouslySetInnerHTML and v-html, at URL attributes where a javascript: href renders happily, at values templated into inline script blocks, and at anything handed to a third-party widget.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Grep the codebase for the framework's named escape hatches and audit each occurrence individually.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: HttpOnly cookies make an XSS survivable.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: HttpOnly stops exfiltration of the identifier, which is worth having — the attacker cannot take the session home and use it next week. It does nothing about the attacker acting as the user right now, because the browser attaches the cookie to the injected script's requests regardless of who wrote that script.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Separate 'read the credential' from 'use the credential' explicitly, and list which actions remain available under each.

competencies.title: Injection and the code/data boundary
competencies.description: See the single root cause behind SQL, NoSQL, command and template injection, and remove it with parameterization and allowlisting rather than escaping.

desiredOutcomes.description: Parameterize every value and allowlist every identifier, including dynamic sort columns.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Adversarial input survives intact in the parameter array and never appears in the query text; unrecognised identifiers are rejected, not sanitised.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Escaping quotes prevents SQL injection.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Escaping patches a broken design instead of fixing it, and fails in ways that are hard to see: it is charset-dependent, it does nothing for unquoted numeric parameters where no quote is needed at all, and it cannot help for identifiers — table names, column names and ORDER BY targets are not string literals, so no quoting makes them safe.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner attempt to escape a dynamic ORDER BY column and discover that the technique does not apply to identifiers at all.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: We use an ORM, so SQL injection is impossible.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: ORMs parameterize the queries they generate, which covers most code. Then every ORM ships escape hatches because real applications need them — raw, literal, whereRaw, queryRawUnsafe — and those take strings. Dynamic column names and string-built where clauses bypass the protection while still looking like ORM code.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Grep the project for the ORM's raw-query methods and review each call site before claiming coverage.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Only user-facing form fields count as untrusted input.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Untrusted means anything you did not compute yourself: headers such as User-Agent and X-Forwarded-For, cookies, uploaded filenames, webhook payloads, third-party API responses — and values previously read back out of your own database that an attacker wrote earlier. That last case is exactly how stored XSS and second-order injection work.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner list every field of a request object and classify each as computed-by-us or influenced-by-someone-else.

competencies.title: Reviewing code for security defects
competencies.description: Find auth, authorization and injection defects in unfamiliar code by tracing trust boundaries, and rank findings so the important ones get fixed.

desiredOutcomes.description: Review unfamiliar code and produce findings ranked by exploitability and blast radius.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Finds at least one missing check (not just a dangerous call), and every finding states reachability and impact.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Security review means scanning the code for dangerous functions like eval and innerHTML.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That is a useful first pass and then it stops. Most real defects are missing checks — an absent ownership comparison, a route added below the middleware, a swallowed authorization error — and no tool greps for a line nobody wrote. The reviewer's advantage over the scanner is asking what should be here that isn't.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Review a seeded file where every defect is an omission and no dangerous identifier appears anywhere.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A finding is a finding — report everything with equal urgency.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Reporting an unreachable theoretical issue as loudly as a live authentication bypass is not thoroughness; it is noise that buries the bypass and trains the team to discount security comments. Every finding needs reachability and impact attached, including the ones you mark low.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-rank a flat list of findings on the two axes and notice which item moved furthest.

competencies.title: Attacking and hardening your own application
competencies.description: Plan and execute a scoped attack against your own build, confirm which control actually stopped each attempt, and document what remains.

desiredOutcomes.description: Attack your own application from a checklist and document mechanism-confirmed results.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Every 'attack failed' entry names the control responsible and how it was confirmed; the residual-risk section is non-empty.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: I wrote this app, so I already know where its holes are.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: You know the holes in the design you imagined. Attackers test the paths you never considered, and nobody can deliberately not-consider something on demand. The remedy is mechanical: work from an explicit checklist you did not derive from your own design, so the list supplies the ideas your imagination didn't.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Work the five-item attack checklist in order without improvising, and count how many attempts came from the list rather than from intuition.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: My exploit attempt failed, which proves the defence works.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The attempt may have failed for reasons unrelated to your control: a malformed payload, a framework default, a proxy that stripped a header, a dev-mode difference. Until you disable the control you believe is responsible and watch the attack succeed, you have not identified which line of code is doing the work.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For one failed attempt, temporarily disable the suspected control, confirm the attack now succeeds, and re-enable it — then record both results.

sections.title: Identity and Sessions
sections.description: Establishing a trustworthy identity and transporting it — password storage, session lifecycle, cookie attributes, and the honest trade between sessions and tokens. Teaching domain: **a hospital patient portal**.

learningObjectives.description: Store passwords with a memory-hard hash and per-user salts, and verify them without leaking timing or existence information.
Implement a session lifecycle: issue, rotate on privilege change, and revoke on logout.
Select and justify cookie attributes for a given deployment, and predict each one's effect on transport and cross-site behaviour.
Write a token validator that rejects tampered, expired, wrong-audience and unsigned tokens — in that order.
Design a refresh and revocation strategy, stating explicitly what statelessness was traded away.
Recommend sessions or tokens for a stated architecture and defend the choice against its strongest counterargument.

motivationHooks.prompt: A patient portal has one job it cannot get wrong: when a request arrives asking for Maria Okafor's lab results, the server must be certain it came from Maria — or from a clinician assigned to her. Everything else in the product is decoration on top of that certainty.

Before you start, commit to an answer: a user clicks **Log out**, the cookie vanishes from their browser, and the request returns 200. Is that session over? Write down yes or no — you will find out in a few minutes whether your instinct matches what the server actually believes.

Breach reports keep landing on the same three causes: passwords stored so that offline cracking was cheap, sessions that stayed valid long after they should have died, and tokens that were decoded but never verified. None of these are exotic. All three start with a reasonable-sounding assumption that happens to be false.

The answer is no — and not partially. Clearing a cookie removes one copy of a bearer credential from one browser while the server's session record sits untouched, which means every copy an attacker took still authenticates. If you predicted yes, you were holding the most common session misconception in the industry, and you now have the code that disproves it.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe four things that most teams get wrong:

1. **Password hashing has two jobs, not one.** A salt defeats precomputation; slowness and memory-hardness defeat per-row brute force. Salting a fast hash solves half the problem and feels like solving all of it.
2. **A login endpoint leaks account existence through three channels** — message, status code and duration — and equalising only the message is the most common half-fix.
3. **A session identifier is a bearer credential.** Possession is identity, so logout must delete server-side state and login must rotate the identifier.
4. **Signing is not encryption, and decoding is not validating.** Verify the signature using an algorithm from your configuration, then read claims — never the reverse.
keyTakeaways: Salt defeats precomputation; **slow and memory-hard** defeats brute force. You need both.
Equalise the login failure path's **message, status code and duration** — a dummy hash buys the third.
Possession of a session identifier *is* identity: rotate it at every privilege change, delete it server-side on logout.
`HttpOnly` stops script **reading** the cookie, not **acting** with it.
`SameSite=Lax` is one layer: top-level GETs still carry the cookie, and subdomains are same-site.
Take the signature algorithm from **your configuration**, never from the token's own header.
Statelessness and instant revocation are in direct tension; every real token system reintroduces state somewhere.

learningExperiences.title: Proving who someone is, and keeping it proved

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

By the end of this experience you will be able to:

- Store passwords with a memory-hard hash and per-user salts, and verify them without leaking timing or existence information.
- Implement a session lifecycle: issue, rotate on privilege change, revoke on logout.
- Select and justify cookie attributes for a given deployment, and predict each one's cross-site behaviour.
- Write a token validator that rejects tampered, expired, wrong-audience and unsigned tokens.
- Design a refresh and revocation strategy, stating what statelessness cost you.
- Recommend sessions or tokens for an architecture and defend the choice.

## Why this matters

HTTP has no memory. Every request arrives as a stranger.

The certainty you think you have about who is calling is actually a small piece of data the client hands you — a cookie, a token — and the entire security of the system reduces to two questions: *can an attacker obtain that piece of data?* and *if they do, what stops them from using it?*

This section makes the assumptions behind those two questions explicit, and then kills the false ones. Almost every failure here comes from a senior developer believing something reasonable that happens not to be true.

contentBlocks.title: About the code in this course
contentBlocks.content:
Examples and exercises run in your browser, in a sandbox. **JavaScript works offline.** The **Python** and **SQL** exercises download their runtime the first time you run one, so that first run needs a network connection; afterwards it is cached.

Where an exercise asks you to write tests, the environment is a **Jest-compatible subset** — `describe`, `it`, `expect`, common matchers, `beforeEach`/`afterEach` and `jest.fn`. It is not Jest: there is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers. Every exercise here is built to need none of those.

## An analogy worth keeping

Think of a hotel key card.

The card does not know who you are. The lock does not know who you are either. The card simply *is* authority: whoever holds it opens the door. That is what security people mean by a **bearer credential**, and it explains almost everything that follows.

It explains why you make the card unguessable, why you invalidate it at checkout rather than politely asking for it back, why handing out a new card at check-in matters more than it sounds, and why a card copied at the front desk is indistinguishable from the original. Hold this picture; the rest of the section is mostly consequences of it.

## Key terms for this section

These five carry most of the weight. They are defined in the glossary too, and highlighted wherever they appear.

- **Bearer credential** — a secret where possession alone proves identity.
- **Salt** — a unique, *public* random value per password, defeating precomputation.
- **Memory-hard** — a hash deliberately demanding a lot of RAM per guess, which is what blunts GPUs.
- **User enumeration** — learning whether an account exists from how the system responds.
- **Session fixation** — an attacker planting a session identifier on a victim *before* they log in.

terms.definition: A transformation that is cheap to compute forwards and infeasible to reverse. Password storage needs one of these, not encryption — anything your server can decrypt, a thief with your key can decrypt too.
The tunable cost parameter of a password hash. Set it so one verification takes roughly 100–250 ms on your production hardware, and revisit it every couple of years as hardware improves.

A single secret value mixed into every password hash, stored separately from the database. Sometimes useful *in addition to* per-user salts — never as a replacement, which is the mistake it usually turns out to be.

contentBlocks.content:
## 1. Storing a password you must never learn

Maria registers and types `correct-horse-battery`. You need to check that string again next Tuesday, but you must never be able to produce it — not for support staff, not under subpoena, not for someone who steals your database.

That rules out encryption immediately: if your server can decrypt a password to compare it, so can anyone who takes the key. You want a **one-way function**.

So you reach for a hash, and this is where most teams stop too early:

```
stored = sha256(password)
```

This fails to two *different* attacks, and separating them matters because the fixes are different.

### Attack A — precomputation

SHA-256 is deterministic and public. An attacker computes `sha256("password123")` once and checks it against every row at the same time. Ten million users, one computation — and published rainbow tables mean they often skip even that.

The fix is a **salt**: a unique random value per user, mixed in before hashing. Now every user's hash sits in its own namespace. Cracking Maria's row tells you nothing about anyone else's, and precomputed tables are worthless because they were built without your salt.

### Attack B — speed

Salting does nothing about the second problem. SHA-256 is *designed* to be fast — a modern GPU does billions per second — so an attacker simply brute-forces each row individually. For any password a human chose, that is hours, not centuries.

The fix is a hash that is deliberately expensive: **bcrypt**, **scrypt** or **Argon2**. They take a tunable work factor, and scrypt and Argon2 are additionally **memory-hard** — each guess needs a large block of RAM. Memory is exactly what GPUs and ASICs are short of per core, which is why memory-hardness, not just slowness, is what blunts industrial cracking.

contentBlocks.caption: Two users, the same password, unrelated stored rows — that is the salt doing its job. Run it.
contentBlocks.content:
import hashlib, hmac

def hash_pw(password, salt, iterations=200_000):
    return hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password.encode(), salt, iterations)

h_maria = hash_pw("hunter2", b"salt-for-maria")
h_david = hash_pw("hunter2", b"salt-for-david")

print("same password, different salts, equal hashes?", h_maria == h_david)
print("verify correct password:", hmac.compare_digest(h_maria, hash_pw("hunter2", b"salt-for-maria")))
print("verify wrong password:", hmac.compare_digest(h_maria, hash_pw("hunter3", b"salt-for-maria")))
print("digest length in bytes:", len(h_maria))

contentBlocks.title: Why PBKDF2 here
contentBlocks.content: PBKDF2 is used in these examples because it is in Python's standard library and runs anywhere. In production prefer **Argon2id** or **scrypt**, which are memory-hard. PBKDF2 is slow but not memory-hard, which is a meaningful difference against GPU attackers.

## Common errors in credential handling

Three beliefs cause most of the damage. Each sounds reasonable, which is the problem.

**"SHA-256 with a salt is fine."** The salt fixed precomputation. It did nothing about speed, and speed is what makes per-row cracking cheap. If your hash takes microseconds, you have handed an attacker billions of guesses per second.

**"Salts are secret."** They are not, and never were. A salt is stored in plaintext beside the hash — it has to be, or you could not verify a login. Believing otherwise pushes teams toward a single global value, which reintroduces exactly the attack salts exist to prevent.

**"Matching error messages stop enumeration."** Matching text closes one channel of three. The status code is machine-readable, and the response *duration* differs because the 'no such user' path skips the expensive hash. A timing oracle is every bit as scriptable as a message.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram: two login requests side by side. The left path finds no user and returns in 0.1 ms; the right path finds a user, spends 200 ms hashing, and returns. Both return the identical message 'Invalid email or password' and an identical 401 status — but a stopwatch beside each path shows the two durations differ by a factor of two thousand, labelled 'the channel you forgot'.

contentBlocks.content:
### Before you continue

You now have the two attacks on stored passwords and the three channels a login endpoint leaks through. The next segment turns a credential that was proved *once* into one that survives four hundred more requests — and that is where the bearer-credential idea starts doing real work.

## 2. From credentials to sessions

Maria has proved who she is, once. She is about to make four hundred more requests. Re-sending the password each time would be absurd, so you issue her something to present instead: a **session identifier**, a long random opaque string stored server-side against her user record.

The property to internalise: that identifier is a **bearer credential**. Whoever holds it *is* Maria, to your server. Not 'is probably Maria' — *is*. There is no second factor inside the string.

Everything else follows from that one fact. The identifier must be:

- **Unguessable** — from a cryptographically secure source, 128+ bits. Never a counter, never a hash of the user id, never a UUIDv1 (which encodes time and a MAC address).
- **Confidential in transit** — hence `Secure`, hence HTTPS everywhere.
- **Unreadable by page scripts** — hence `HttpOnly`.
- **Revocable** — because bearer credentials get stolen and invalidation is your only recourse.
- **Rotated at privilege boundaries** — see below.

### Session fixation, and why rotation is not optional

An attacker visits your portal and is issued an anonymous session `S`. They trick Maria into using `S` — a crafted link, a cookie scoped from a sibling subdomain, an XSS on a neighbouring app. Maria logs in. If your server keeps the same identifier and merely attaches her user id to it, the attacker is now holding a session that authenticates **as Maria**.

The fix is one line: issue a brand-new identifier at every privilege change — login, elevation to admin, step-up authentication — and destroy the old one.

contentBlocks.title: Misconception check: "logging out on the client is logging out"
contentBlocks.content:
Deleting the cookie in the browser removes one *copy* of a bearer credential. The server-side session is still valid, and any copy an attacker made still authenticates — which also means a "log out all devices" feature built this way does nothing at all.

**Logout is a server-side delete.** Clearing the cookie is tidying up afterwards. You are about to predict the output of eight lines that make this concrete, so commit to an answer before you run it.

## 3. Cookie attributes, precisely

Cookies are how the identifier travels. Each attribute does one specific job, and vague understanding here is the source of an enormous number of production holes. The right-hand column is the one worth memorising.

contentBlocks.caption: What each attribute does — and, more usefully, what it does not.
rows: Hides the value from `document.cookie`, so injected script cannot read it.
Stop injected script *making requests as the user* — the browser still attaches the cookie.
Prevents the cookie being sent over plain HTTP.
Encrypt the value, or protect it from a compromised browser.
Withholds the cookie on all cross-site requests, including top-level navigation.
Work well for portals reached from emailed links — the user arrives apparently logged out.
Sends on top-level GET navigations; withholds on cross-site POST, iframes and fetches.
Protect state-changing **GET** endpoints, or defend against a compromised sibling subdomain, which is same-site.
Allows full cross-site sending. **Requires `Secure`** or browsers reject the cookie outright.
Anything protective — this is the opt-*out*.
Narrow where the cookie is sent. `Domain=.hospital.test` *widens* it to every subdomain.
Provide isolation — a widened `Domain` ships your session to every subdomain, including ones other people operate.
Control the server-side lifetime — that is yours to enforce separately, and it is the one that matters.

contentBlocks.content:
## 4. The other design: signed tokens

Instead of keeping session state server-side, you can hand the client a **JWT**: three base64url segments — header, payload, signature — where the signature covers the first two.

Two consequences follow immediately, and senior developers get both wrong with surprising regularity.

### The payload is readable

base64url is an *encoding*, not encryption. Anyone holding the token reads every claim. Never put anything in a JWT you would not print on the outside of an envelope — in a hospital that includes diagnosis codes, clinic names and usually the user's role.

Signing gives you **integrity** and **origin**: nobody altered it, and it came from a key holder. It gives you nothing on confidentiality, and nothing on *freshness* — a token minted before Maria's account was suspended stays valid until it expires.

### Decoding is not validating

`jwt.decode()` in several libraries parses without checking anything. A real validator checks, in this order:

1. **Structure** — three segments, parseable header.
2. **Algorithm** — against *your configuration*, never the token's own `alg` header.
3. **Signature** — compared in constant time over the exact signing input.
4. **`exp` / `nbf`** — in **seconds**, not milliseconds, with a small clock-skew allowance.
5. **`iss` and `aud`** — a token minted for your analytics service must not open the records API.
6. **Revocation state** — if you have any.

Step 2 is the one that gets skipped. Accepting `alg: none` means accepting unsigned tokens; accepting `HS256` where you expected `RS256` lets an attacker sign with your **public** key as the HMAC secret. The token must never tell your validator how to check it.

contentBlocks.title: About the token exercise you are about to do
contentBlocks.content:
Real HMAC needs crypto APIs that are awkward inside a browser sandbox, so the exercise substitutes a deterministic **toy signature function** and URI-encoded segments for base64url. Everything the exercise actually tests — the *order* of checks, taking the algorithm from configuration, failing closed — is identical to the real thing.

What the toy cannot teach you is the cryptography itself. In production, use a maintained library, pass it an explicit algorithm allowlist, and never write your own comparison.

## Summary

- Password storage needs a **slow, memory-hard** hash plus a **per-user salt**. Salts are public; slowness is the security property.
- A login endpoint leaks account existence through **message, status code and timing**. Equalise all three; a dummy hash buys you the third.
- Compare secrets in **constant time**.
- A session identifier is a **bearer credential**: possession is identity. Make it unguessable, `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, revocable — and **rotate it at every privilege change** to kill fixation.
- Cookie attributes each do one job. `HttpOnly` stops reading, not acting. `SameSite=Lax` is a layer, not a solution. A widened `Domain` shares your session with every subdomain.
- **Logout is a server-side delete.**
- JWT payloads are readable; signatures give integrity, not confidentiality or freshness.
- Take the algorithm from **your config**. Verify, then read claims.
- Statelessness and revocation are in tension. Short access tokens plus rotating server-side refresh tokens is the standard compromise; a hard revocation deadline forces real state.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Commit to a prediction before running this. Both lines print something — write down what, and why.

The `Map` is your server's session store. `clientCookie` is the browser's copy of the identifier. The browser then "logs out".

codeExercise.explanation:
It prints `true` and `7`.

The mental model most developers carry is that the cookie *is* the session, so discarding the cookie feels like destroying the session. It isn't and it doesn't. `clientCookie` held a **copy of a key**, not the session object; setting it to `null` changes one variable in one place and leaves the server's `Map` entirely untouched.

Now map it back: the variable is the browser, the `Map` is your session store, and an attacker who copied the identifier earlier — from a shared machine, a proxy log, a stolen backup — still holds a working key to a live session.

This is the whole argument for logout being a server-side delete, and it is also why "log out all devices" is nothing more exotic than deleting every entry for that user.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The session outlived the cookie. If your prediction was `false` and an error, you were reasoning about the browser; the server never heard about any of it.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Your session cookie is `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`. An attacker achieves stored XSS on your site — their script runs on your origin, in your user's browser.

What have those attributes actually prevented?
options: Nothing — HttpOnly is useless once script runs in your origin.
The attacker cannot act as the user, because the cookie is unreadable.
Theft of the identifier, but not the attacker issuing authenticated requests from inside the page.
Both theft and use, because SameSite=Lax also blocks the injected script's requests.

optionFeedback.feedback: An overcorrection. `HttpOnly` genuinely does stop `document.cookie` from reading the identifier, which blocks exfiltration — the attacker cannot take the session home and use it next week.
Unreadable is not unusable. The browser attaches the cookie to every request the injected script makes, so the attacker acts as the user without ever seeing the value.
Correct, and this is exactly the boundary of `HttpOnly`: it stops **reading**, not **acting**. Exfiltration is convenient for an attacker; on-page action is usually sufficient.
The injected script runs on *your* origin, so its requests are same-site and `SameSite` has no opinion about them at all.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Keep this boundary sharp, because section three turns on it. `HttpOnly` splits the attacker's options into *steal the credential* and *use the credential*, and closes only the first. Most attacks only need the second.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Rank these four login implementations from **most** to **least** resistant to user enumeration.

Drag the best to the top.
options: Identical message, identical status code, dummy hash computed when the user is absent.
Identical message and status code, but returns immediately when the user is absent.
Identical message, but HTTP 404 for an unknown user and 401 for a wrong password.
Distinct messages: "No account with that email" and "Incorrect password".

optionFeedback.feedback: Best. It equalises all three channels — message, status and duration. The dummy hash is what buys the third, and it is the one people leave out.
Second. The visible channels are closed, but the timing gap between a 0.1 ms miss and a 200 ms hash is a clean, scriptable oracle.
Third. A status code is machine-readable, so this leaks just as reliably as text — it merely looks tidier in the browser.
Worst. It leaks in plain language and requires no skill whatsoever to exploit at scale.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The interesting boundary is between the top two. Both look identical to a human using the site; only one looks identical to a script with a stopwatch.

If you placed the immediate-return version first, that is the most common half-fix in this area — the belief that matching text is sufficient when duration is also a channel. The same reasoning extends to password reset ("if that email is registered, we've sent a link" — always, regardless) and to lockout counters, which are themselves an enumeration signal unless paired with per-IP limits.

interactionSequence.prompt:
**Equalise the login failure path.**

Return `"Signed in"` only when the user exists *and* the password matches. Every failure — wrong password, no such account — returns the identical string `"Invalid email or password"`.

The harder requirement is invisible to the checker and is the real lesson: both paths must do the **same amount of work**, so hash unconditionally, even when there is no user. Compare with `hmac.compare_digest`, never `==`.

This is Python, so the first run downloads the runtime. Expect to iterate.

codeExercise.starterCode:
import hashlib, hmac

DUMMY_SALT = "dummy-salt-for-absent-users"
DUMMY_HASH = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", b"no-such-user", DUMMY_SALT.encode(), 1000).hex()

def hash_pw(password, salt):
    return hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password.encode(), salt.encode(), 1000).hex()

def login_message(user_exists, stored_password, candidate):
    # [[edit]]
    # Pick a salt and a stored hash. When there is no user, fall back to the
    # dummy values above so this path costs the same as the real one.
    salt = None
    stored = None
    # Hash the candidate unconditionally, compare in constant time,
    # then return one of the two messages.
    return ""
    # [[/edit]]
codeExercise.solutionNote:
Note the shape: **no early return**. The temptation is `if not user_exists: return "Invalid email or password"` at the top, which passes every test case here and reintroduces the timing oracle in full. Both facts — the user existed, and the digests matched — are computed first and combined at the very end.

In production the same structure applies, with Argon2id or scrypt in place of PBKDF2 and a work factor you have actually measured.

cases.name: correct password for an existing user
wrong password for an existing user
no such account — must be indistinguishable

hints: Both branches — user found and user absent — must execute the same expensive operation. What does that tell you about where an `if` can safely go?
`hmac.compare_digest` exists precisely because `==` returns early at the first differing byte. Use it for the comparison.
You need two facts to return "Signed in": the user existed, and the digests matched. Compute both, then combine them on the last line.
feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The checker can only see your return values. A reviewer — and an attacker with a stopwatch — sees the shape of the function.

If you wrote an early return for the missing-user case, your tests pass and your endpoint still answers the question "does this email have an account here?" in about 0.1 ms versus 200 ms. In a hospital context that leak is itself the breach, before any password is guessed.

interactionSequence.prompt:
**Build the `Set-Cookie` value.**

Assemble the attributes in this order: `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite`, `Path`, `Max-Age`. Include `Path` always, defaulting to `/`. Return the literal string `"INVALID"` for the one combination browsers reject outright.

One test case is the whole exercise. Look for it.

codeExercise.solutionNote:
The deletion-cookie case is the one that matters. `Max-Age=0` is how you tell a browser to discard a cookie *now* — and `if (opts.maxAge)` silently drops it, because `0` is falsy. The result is a "logout" that never expires anything in the browser, written by someone who believed they had logged the user out.

Check **presence**, not truthiness: `opts.maxAge !== undefined`.

cases.name: boundary: Max-Age=0 deletion cookie must still appear
SameSite=None is fine once Secure is set

hints: Case 2 is the exercise. `Max-Age=0` is a real, meaningful value — what does `if (opts.maxAge)` do with the number zero?
Distinguish "absent" from "present and falsy". Which comparison does that?
The SameSite=None rule is a hard browser requirement, not a preference — check it before building anything.
feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Two traps, both quiet. Dropping `Max-Age=0` produces a logout the browser never hears about. Emitting `SameSite=None` without `Secure` produces a cookie the browser discards on arrival — your server sends it happily, nothing logs an error, and users simply appear logged out at random.

interactionSequence.prompt:
**Write a token validator that fails closed.**

Return `{ valid: true, claims }` or `{ valid: false, reason }`, where `reason` is one of `"malformed"`, `"alg"`, `"signature"`, `"expired"`, `"audience"` — checked **in that order**.

The order is the specification, not a style preference. `exp` means "not valid at or after this instant". The helpers are provided; the whole body is yours this time.

codeExercise.solutionNote:
Two details carry the security.

**The algorithm comes from `config`, never from `header.alg`.** Compare the header's value against your expectation and reject on mismatch — do not use it to select a verification routine. That single habit kills both the `alg: none` attack and the RS256-to-HS256 downgrade.

**Nothing in the payload is read until the signature has passed.** The `exp` and `aud` checks sit *below* the signature check for that reason. A validator that reads `payload.role` first is not a validator; it is a parser an attacker configures.

In production, use a maintained library and pass it an explicit algorithm allowlist. In real JWTs `exp` is in **seconds** — comparing it against a millisecond clock is a classic bug that usually gets "fixed" by flipping the comparison, producing a validator that accepts everything.

cases.name: attack: signed with the wrong key

hints: Which check must come before you trust *anything* inside the payload? Put that one above the `exp` and `aud` checks.
The alg-none case passes trivially if you read the algorithm from the token and use it. Where should the algorithm come from instead?
`exp` means "not valid at or after this instant". When `exp` equals `nowSeconds`, the token is already expired — which comparison operator gives you that?
feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Notice what the failing cases have in common: each one is a token an attacker can construct without your signing key. `alg: none` removes the signature entirely; the wrong-key token is what someone else's key produces; the analytics token is one your own system legitimately minted for a different audience.

A validator is not a parser with checks bolted on afterwards. It is a gate whose order is the design.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Think about a system you have actually worked on that used tokens.

What happened when someone needed to be locked out immediately — a departing employee, a compromised account, a role downgrade? Was there a real mechanism, or did everyone quietly wait for expiry and hope?

Write a few sentences. You are not being graded on the answer; you are being asked to check a belief against a memory.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Most people find one of three things: there was no mechanism and expiry was short enough that nobody noticed; there was a denylist, which means state was reintroduced and someone decided that was acceptable; or there was a mechanism that had never actually been tested.

All three are defensible engineering positions. What is not defensible is the fourth case — believing revocation works because the design said "tokens" and nobody checked. That belief is the misconception this section targets, and it usually surfaces on the worst possible day.

interactionSequence.prompt:
**Practical decision.** The portal is expanding. There are now three clients:

- a browser SPA at `portal.hospital.test`, talking to `api.hospital.test`
- a clinician mobile app, used on hospital-issued tablets
- a nightly batch service that pulls anonymised data for research

Compliance adds one hard requirement: **a suspended clinician must lose all access within 60 seconds.**

Write your design. Specify, for each client, whether you issue a session cookie or a token and why; how you meet the 60-second requirement; and what you gave up to meet it. Then state the strongest argument *against* your own design and answer it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
A strong answer usually lands near this shape.

**Browser SPA: session cookie.** Same-site deployment, `HttpOnly` keeps the credential out of JavaScript's reach entirely — something `localStorage` cannot offer — and revocation is a row delete.

**Mobile app: tokens.** No cookie jar you control, and the app may talk to more than one service. Short access tokens (5 minutes) plus a rotating, server-stored refresh token.

**Batch service: its own credential**, not a user token. A client credential scoped to exactly the dataset it reads.

**The 60-second requirement is the interesting part.** Five-minute access tokens do not meet it. You need a revocation check on the request path — a `jti` denylist, cached in memory, holding only tokens revoked within the last access-token lifetime, so it stays small. You have now reintroduced server state on every request, and that is precisely the honest trade: *statelessness was the thing you gave up to meet the deadline.*

**The strongest counterargument** is that the denylist lookup is a new dependency in the hot path and a new failure mode — if it is unavailable, do you fail open or closed? Answer it explicitly. (Fail closed, and treat denylist availability as a tier-one dependency.)

One bonus most people miss: rotating refresh tokens give you **theft detection**. If the same refresh token is presented twice, a copy exists, and you can revoke the entire family — something a purely stateless design can never do.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Close the loop in your own words.

Explain to a colleague who has not taken this course what a **bearer credential** is, and then use that single idea to explain *three* separate design rules from this section. Do not use the phrase "because it's more secure" — say what specifically goes wrong without each rule.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Here is the version worth comparing against.

A bearer credential is a secret where **possession alone proves identity** — there is no second check inside the string, so your server cannot distinguish the legitimate holder from anyone who obtained a copy.

That single property generates the rules:

1. **Rotate at login.** If a pre-login identifier survives authentication, an attacker who planted it now possesses an authenticated credential. Fixation is only possible because possession is sufficient.
2. **Delete server-side on logout.** The user's browser forgetting its copy does not affect any other copy. The only way to end a bearer credential's life is to stop honouring it.
3. **`HttpOnly` and `Secure`.** Both exist to reduce the number of places a copy can be made — out of JavaScript's reach, off plaintext networks. Neither helps once a copy exists, which is why revocation is not optional.

If you can generate those three from the one idea, you will generate the fourth and fifth yourself when you meet them.

workedExamples.title: Verifying a password without leaking
steps: **Identify leak 1 — the message.** The two error strings differ. An attacker with ten million email addresses can now sort them into "has an account at this hospital" and "doesn't". For a hospital that is a privacy breach on its own, before any password is guessed. This is **user enumeration**.

**Identify leak 2 — the comparison.** `==` on bytes short-circuits at the first differing byte. The difference is tiny but measurable across many samples, and it lets an attacker recover the stored hash incrementally. Use a **constant-time comparison**: `hmac.compare_digest` in Python, `crypto.timingSafeEqual` in Node.

**Identify leak 3 — the one you did not look for.** Even with identical messages and identical status codes, the *no such user* branch returns immediately while the *user exists* branch spends 200 ms hashing. The response time is itself the enumeration oracle. Fix it by hashing anyway, against a dummy salt, so both paths cost the same.

**Rewrite so that no branch is free.**

```python
DUMMY_SALT = b"dummy-salt-constant"

def login(email, password):
    user = db.find_user(email)
    salt = user.salt if user else DUMMY_SALT
    stored = user.hash if user else DUMMY_HASH
    candidate = hash_pw(password, salt)          # always paid
    ok = hmac.compare_digest(candidate, stored)  # constant-time
    if user and ok:
        return {"ok": True}
    return {"error": "Invalid email or password"}   # identical for both failures
```

**Check the shape, not just the output.** There is no early return. Both facts — the user existed, the digests matched — are computed, then combined on the last line. That structure is what makes the two paths indistinguishable.
workedExamples.conclusion:
Correct credential handling is **three** things, not one: a slow memory-hard hash, a per-user salt, and a verification path whose message, status code and duration are identical whether or not the account exists.

The same reasoning extends beyond login. Password reset should say "if that email is registered, we've sent a link" — always, regardless. And per-account lockout counters are themselves an enumeration signal unless paired with per-IP limits.

givenSteps: **Given — the message leak.** The two responses differ in text and in shape (`error` versus `ok`), so an attacker learns directly whether each address is registered.
**Given — the fix for the message.** Return the identical response in both cases: `{"ok": True, "message": "If that address is registered, we've sent a link."}` — regardless of what was found.
**Given — the remaining worry.** Sending an email is slow and variable, which means the timing channel here behaves differently from the login case and needs its own treatment.
blankedStepPrompts: The message is now identical, but one branch still does noticeably more work than the other. Describe the timing leak that remains, and give a concrete fix that does not require sending an email to non-existent users.

There is a second, non-timing channel unique to this endpoint that still reveals which addresses are registered — one that no change inside this function can close. Name it, and say what you would do about it.
blankedStepAnswers: The registered branch sends an email — network I/O measured in hundreds of milliseconds — while the unregistered branch returns almost instantly. Queue the work instead of doing it inline: push a job and return immediately in **both** cases, so the response time reflects the queue write, not the email. (Pushing a no-op job for unknown addresses keeps the two paths symmetric.) An alternative is a fixed response delay, but that wastes a request slot and is easy to get subtly wrong.

**Rate limiting and observable side effects.** An attacker who controls a mail server can still distinguish registered addresses by whether mail arrives — nothing inside this handler can prevent that. What you can do is make the probing expensive: per-IP rate limits on this endpoint, a CAPTCHA or proof-of-work after a threshold, and alerting on high-volume enumeration patterns. This is the honest limit of the technique: you close the channels you own, then raise the cost of the one you don't.

workedExamples.title: Choosing cookie attributes for a real deployment
workedExamples.problem:
Decide the exact `Set-Cookie` attributes for the portal's session.

The deployment: `portal.hospital.test` serves the UI, `api.hospital.test` serves the API, and `blog.hospital.test` is a marketing site run by an outside agency. Appointment-reminder emails contain deep links into the portal.
steps: **`Secure`?** Yes, unconditionally. Everything is HTTPS, and there is no scenario in which you want this credential on a plaintext connection.

**`HttpOnly`?** Yes. No front-end code has a legitimate reason to read a session identifier. This closes exfiltration if you ever suffer an XSS — though, as you saw, it does not stop an attacker acting inside the page.

**`Domain`?** Tempting: setting `Domain=.hospital.test` would let the cookie reach the API host. But it would also ship Maria's session to the agency's blog on **every single request**. Do not. Either host the API under the same origin behind a path prefix, or accept a cross-origin design and configure it explicitly.

**`SameSite`?** `Lax`. `Strict` would break the "view your results" links in appointment emails — patients would arrive apparently logged out. That is a real usability cost, and the kind that gets the setting reverted by someone in a hurry at 5pm on a Friday. `Lax` plus explicit CSRF defences is the choice that survives contact with the organisation.
**Lifetime?** Set a modest `Max-Age`, and enforce an independent server-side expiry. The browser's copy is a convenience; the server's record is the authority.
workedExamples.conclusion:
`Set-Cookie: sid=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/` — with **no** `Domain` attribute, so the cookie stays host-only.

Notice that two of the five decisions were driven by non-security concerns: email deep links and the agency's blog. Attribute choices that ignore how the organisation actually works get reverted, and a reverted control protects nobody.
