A developer escapes angle brackets in a nickname before putting it in an `alt` attribute. Predict the exact output line — and decide whether the result is safe.

The nickname contains no `<` and no `>`.

codeExercise.explanation: It prints ``. The mental shorthand for XSS is "an attacker injects a `

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: If you predicted the text but thought it was safe, that is the more interesting miss: you read the output correctly and did not see that `onmouseover` is now a live attribute of the developer's own tag.

interactionSequence.prompt: Your team proposes HTML-escaping all user input at the API boundary, before storing it. What is the **strongest** objection?
options: It is too slow to escape on every write.
The correct encoding depends on the output context, which is unknown at input time — and pre-escaping corrupts the value for every non-HTML consumer.
It works for HTML, but a Content-Security-Policy is a better substitute.
It is unnecessary, because modern frameworks auto-escape everything.

optionFeedback.feedback: Performance is negligible here and beside the point — the objection is about correctness, not cost.
Correct, and it is strongest because it is two independent arguments at once: contexts differ and are unknowable in advance, and stored data serves more consumers than the web page.
CSP mitigates the damage of an injection; it does not replace encoding. And the objection to input-escaping stands whether or not a CSP exists.
Auto-escaping covers text interpolation and stops at named escape hatches — raw-HTML props, URL attributes, inline script blocks.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The data-corruption half is the one that wins arguments with people who are not security-minded, because it produces bugs they already care about: `O'Brien` printed on a physical ticket, in a CSV export opened in a spreadsheet, and in the door-scanning app at the venue.

A rule that only security people can defend gets reverted. A rule that also prevents ugly tickets survives.

interactionSequence.prompt:
An attacker achieves stored XSS on a site using `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` session cookies **and** per-request CSRF tokens.

What is the realistic impact?
options: Minimal — the cookie cannot be read and SameSite=Strict blocks the forged requests.
Limited to defacement, since the attacker cannot authenticate as the user.
Full compromise within the origin — the script reads CSRF tokens from the DOM and performs authenticated actions, even though it cannot read the cookie.
Serious only if the CSRF token is kept in localStorage rather than in the DOM.

optionFeedback.feedback: The injected script runs on **your** origin, so its requests are same-site and carry the cookie normally. SameSite has no opinion about them.
No authentication is needed: the requests are made by the user's own browser with the user's own live session attached.
Correct. HttpOnly blocks exfiltration, not on-page action — and that distinction is the whole ranking of XSS severity.
The storage location is irrelevant; script running in your origin reaches either one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
This is the moment the course's three sections collapse into one picture. Every credential protection from section one and every CSRF layer from section two is bypassed at once — not broken, bypassed, because the requests genuinely are the user's.

What survives? Two things: per-action **re-authentication** on destructive operations, and the **authorization** layer — an attacker riding a student's session still cannot do what a student cannot do. That is why authorization is independent of CSRF defence rather than an alternative to it.

interactionSequence.prompt: You are writing up a review. Rank these four findings by the priority you would assign — highest first.
options: An unauthenticated endpoint returning any user's order history by id.
A stored XSS in a display name rendered on every public listing page.
SQL injection in an admin-only report filter, reachable by three staff accounts.
A missing Vary: Origin header on an otherwise correctly allowlisted CORS response.

optionFeedback.feedback: Highest: no barrier at all and a blast radius of every user. Unauthenticated plus everyone's data is the worst square on the grid.
Second: compromises every viewer's session within the origin, gated only by someone loading a page — which, on a public listing page, is not much of a gate.
Third: catastrophic blast radius, but it requires an already-privileged account, so exploitability is materially lower.
Lowest: a real caching defect worth fixing, with no direct path to compromise given a correct allowlist.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The instructive comparison is the SQL injection. On blast radius alone it is arguably the worst thing on the list — and it still ranks third, because three staff accounts is a real barrier that the first two findings simply do not have.

Ranking on impact alone puts it first, which is the "a finding is a finding" failure in a subtler form: weighting severity while ignoring reachability. Both axes, every time.

interactionSequence.prompt:
**Write a context-aware encoder.**

`encodeFor(context, value)` handles three contexts and refuses the rest:

- `"html"` — escape `&`, `<`, `>`
- `"attr"` — escape `&`, `<`, `>`, `"`, `'`
- `"url"` — `encodeURIComponent`
- anything else — return `""` (fail closed)

`null` and `undefined` become `""`. Watch the order of your replacements.

codeExercise.solutionNote:
**Escape `&` first.** If you replace it last, the `&` you just introduced by escaping `<` gets escaped again and you emit `&lt;` — the user sees literal `<` on the page. Classic double-encoding.

**Two cases use the same payload in different contexts** and expect different answers: the attribute encoder neutralises `" onmouseover="go()` while the HTML encoder deliberately leaves the quote alone. That is not an inconsistency — it is the entire point. A bare `"` in an HTML body is inert.

**The unknown context returns `""`.** Failing closed on a context whose rules you do not know beats guessing and emitting something dangerous.

In production, prefer your framework's context-aware escaping over hand-rolled encoders. The value of writing one is understanding why there is no single `sanitize()`.

cases.name: script tag in an HTML body
attribute breakout is neutralised in attr context
same payload in html context: the quote is left alone, and that is correct

hints: Two cases pass the *same* payload with different contexts and expect different results. What does that tell you about where the decision belongs?
The 'Tom & Jerry' case fails if you replace `&` last — think about the `&` you create when you escape `<`.
For an unknown context you do not know the rules, so you cannot encode safely. What is the safe thing to return?
feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Now notice what this function **cannot** do. Run it on `javascript:alert(1)` in any of its three contexts and the string comes back essentially unchanged, because it contains no HTML metacharacters at all.

URLs need a parser and a scheme allowlist, not an escaper. That is why the lecture's `safeUrl` is a separate tool rather than a fourth branch here — and it is the single most common gap in hand-rolled XSS defences.

**Build a safe dynamic query.**

Return `{ sql, params }` for an order search. Every **value** goes in `params` behind a `?`. The sort column comes from `SORT_COLUMNS`, defaulting to `created_at`; the direction is `DESC` only when `dir` is exactly `"desc"`, otherwise `ASC`.

Filters are optional. `email` uses `LIKE` with `%` either side; `eventId` uses `=`. When both are present they are joined with `AND`, in that order.

No filters at all means no `WHERE` clause.

codeExercise.solutionNote:
Look at what happens to the injection payload in case 2: `"%' OR 1=1 --%"` appears **intact** in `params` and **nowhere** in `sql`. That pair of facts is the definition of parameterization. The data survives unaltered; it simply never enters the instruction channel.

A solution that strips quotes from `filters.email` instead of binding it would also pass — and would have broken every buyer named O'Brien while fixing nothing, because the payload was never the problem. The *channel* was.

For the sort column and direction, the user's input never reaches the query at all: it selects a key in your map, or it is discarded. Cases 3 and 4 cannot be solved by escaping, because identifiers and keywords are not string literals.

cases.name: injection in a value: survives in params, absent from sql

expected.sql: SELECT id, buyer_name, total_cents FROM orders WHERE buyer_email LIKE ? ORDER BY created_at ASC

cases.name: injection in the sort column: allowlist rejects it

SELECT id, buyer_name, total_cents FROM orders ORDER BY created_at ASC
SELECT id, buyer_name, total_cents FROM orders WHERE buyer_email LIKE ? AND event_id = ? ORDER BY created_at ASC

Cases 3 and 4 cannot be solved by escaping. What structure lets a user choose a column without ever supplying one?
Case 5 is about ordering: the params array must line up positionally with the `?` marks in the order they appear in the SQL.
feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
You have now used both techniques in one function, which is the realistic shape: **parameterize the values, allowlist the identifiers**.

Notice that neither technique involved inspecting the user's input for dangerous content. That is the deeper point — you never had to decide what a dangerous character is, which means you cannot get that decision wrong.

interactionSequence.prompt:
**Allowlist the scheme.**

`safeUrl(raw)` returns the resolved URL when its scheme is `http:`, `https:` or `mailto:`, and the string `"#"` otherwise — including for anything unparseable, empty or null.

Resolve relative URLs against `https://tickets.example`.

No scaffolding this time. You have done the faded version; this is the independent one.

codeExercise.solutionNote:
Three design choices are doing the work.

**Allowlist, not blocklist.** A blocklist of `javascript:` is defeated by `JaVaScRiPt:`, by embedded tabs and control characters, by leading whitespace, and by `data:text/html;base64,…`. The allowlist needs no such enumeration: anything not on the list is refused, including schemes invented after you wrote the code.

**Structured parsing, not string matching.** `new URL()` normalises case and whitespace for you, which is why the mixed-case and leading-space cases pass without special handling.

**A harmless failure value.** Returning `"#"` rather than throwing means a malformed link renders as a dead link instead of taking down the page — and nobody wraps it in a `try/catch` that silently swallows the problem.

The empty-string case is the subtle one: `new URL("", base)` succeeds and resolves to the base URL, so without the early guard an empty href would silently become a link to your homepage.

leading whitespace does not evade it either
a legitimate https URL survives with its query string
relative path resolves against the base

hints: Three cases are the same attack with different disguises — mixed case, leading whitespace, a different scheme. Is there one check that handles all three without enumerating them?
`new URL()` throws on unparseable input. What should happen then, and what should happen for an empty string that does *not* throw?
Compare against `u.protocol`, which the parser has already normalised for you — do not pattern-match the raw string.
feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
This is the third time this course has reached for the same tool. `ORDER BY` columns, CORS origins, URL schemes — whenever the safe set is small and enumerable, **enumerate it and refuse everything else**.

Blocklists fail for a structural reason, not a tuning reason: they require you to predict every dangerous input, and attackers are specifically in the business of finding the one you did not predict.

interactionSequence.prompt:
**Fix the broken search so the given tests pass.**

Three defects: the seller name is concatenated into the SQL, the sort column is taken straight from user input, and nothing is passed as parameters at all.

The tests are the specification. Note the second one in particular — it asserts both where the payload *is* and where it is *not*.

(Jest-compatible subset: `describe`, `it`, `expect`, `beforeEach`, `jest.fn`. No module mocking, no fake timers.)

codeExercise.solutionNote:
**The second test is the one to study.** It asserts the payload appears in `params` and does *not* appear in `sql`. Together those two assertions are the definition of parameterization — and separately, neither would be sufficient.

A learner who makes that test pass by stripping quotes from the input has broken every seller named O'Brien and has fixed nothing: the value was never dangerous, the channel was.

**The sort allowlist defaults rather than throws.** `SORTS[filters.sort] || "id"` turns an unrecognised column into the safe default. Throwing is also defensible — what is not defensible is passing it through.

Note that `ORDER BY` is appended unconditionally, so the no-filters case still gets a deterministic order. Unordered result sets paginate incorrectly, which is a correctness bug hiding inside a security fix.

hints: `db.query` takes a second argument. Two of the five tests inspect it.
For the sort column, no amount of escaping will do — you need a map from user-supplied keys to column names you wrote yourself.
The last test calls with no filters and still expects an `ORDER BY`. Should that clause be inside an `if`?
feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
You have now fixed the same class of bug in two directions: writing safe code from scratch, and repairing unsafe code against a specification you did not write. The second is closer to the job.

One caution carried over from section two: a passing suite is evidence about behaviour, never a complete security argument. These tests cannot see whether you left a *second* concatenation somewhere else in the file — which is exactly what the review exercise below asks you to look for.

There are six findings here. Ranked:

**1 — The swallowed authorization check (critical, unauthenticated).** `requireRole` throws, the `catch` logs a warning, and execution continues to issue the refund. This endpoint is effectively unauthenticated — there is no `requireLogin` either, so `req.user` may be undefined entirely. Anyone who can reach the route can refund any order.

**2 — SQL injection in `orderId` (critical, whole database).** Concatenated directly, and unquoted, so it does not even need a quote character: `1 OR 1=1` is enough. Reachable by the same unauthenticated caller as finding 1, which is what makes it critical rather than high.

**3 — Stored/reflected XSS into an email (high).** `reason` is interpolated into HTML with no encoding. Email clients vary in what they execute, but the same value is almost certainly rendered in an admin dashboard too — and that is a second sink nobody audited.

**4 — Attacker-controlled recipient (high).** `notifyEmail` comes from the request body. Combined with finding 3 this is an open phishing relay sending attacker-written HTML from your domain, with your reputation attached.

**5 — Full order object returned (medium).** `res.json({ order })` returns every column, likely including payment metadata and internal fields. Return a projection, not the row.

**6 — No idempotency (medium).** Nothing prevents the same refund being issued twice by replaying the request.

**Which defect would grep never have found?** Finding 1. There is no dangerous function name to search for — the defect is that a `throw` was converted into a log line, so the *absence* of a return statement is the vulnerability. A scanner sees a `try/catch` and a logger call, both of which look like good practice.

That is the reviewer's advantage over the tool, and it is why the checklist for this competency is "trace the boundaries and hunt absences" rather than "search for eval".

interactionSequence.prompt:
Look back across all three sections.

Which belief did you personally hold at the start that you no longer hold — and what specifically changed your mind? Be concrete: name the belief, and name the code, output or argument that dislodged it.

If nothing changed, say that instead, and note which claim you are still unconvinced by.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
This is not a formality. Naming the belief you gave up is the single most reliable predictor that the correction survives past the end of a course — and a correction you cannot name tends to decay back into the original intuition within weeks.

The four that most people name: that clearing a cookie logs someone out; that a CORS error means nothing reached the server; that `SameSite=Lax` had closed CSRF; and that `HttpOnly` made XSS survivable.

If you answered "nothing changed", that is a legitimate answer and the second half matters more — an unconvinced reader who names the specific claim they doubt is doing better science than a convinced one who cannot say why. Take that claim into the audit and try to falsify it against your own app.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Explain "injection is one bug" to a colleague who knows SQL injection but has never thought of XSS as related to it.

Use one sentence for the shared root cause, then walk them through **two** different interpreters showing the identical structure. Finish by telling them what to look for in their own code tomorrow — as a search strategy, not a list of vulnerability names.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Compare against this.

**Root cause, one sentence:** attacker-written data crosses into the channel where an interpreter expects instructions, because both were handed over as one flat string.

**SQL:** the database receives `WHERE name = 'O'Brien'` and cannot tell where your instructions resumed. Fix: hand the statement and the values over separately, so parsing finishes before any value is bound.

**HTML:** the browser receives `<div>` plus whatever the user typed and cannot tell where your markup resumed. Fix: transform the value for the specific context it is landing in, so it can only ever be text.

Same structure, same fix shape — separate the channels, or make the crossing impossible.

**The search strategy** is the part that transfers. Tell them: *find every place a string you did not write is concatenated into a string something else will parse.* Not "look for SQL injection" — look for **concatenation into an interpreter**. That one habit finds SQL, HTML, shell, template, LDAP and the injection class invented next year, because it describes the mechanism rather than enumerating its instances.

workedExamples.title: The search endpoint that resisted parameterization
steps: **Spot what is still concatenated.** The `email` filter is correctly bound with `?`. `sortCol` and `dir` are interpolated straight from user input. This is the single most common *partial* fix: parameterize what you can, give up on the rest, and ship.

**Understand why they gave up — they were half right.** It genuinely cannot be parameterized. Placeholders bind **values**, and a column name is not a value. `ORDER BY ?` binds a constant and sorts by nothing at all, which looks like a broken feature rather than a security control.

**Reject the tempting middle path.** Escaping does not apply here either. Identifiers are not string literals, so quoting them does not make them safe, and stripping non-alphanumerics narrows the attack without closing it — `ORDER BY` targets can still be abused for blind data extraction one boolean at a time.

**Name precisely what made it safe.** The interpolated text is no longer derived from user input *at all*. The user's input selects a **key**; the value that reaches the query came from your source code. Unrecognised input is rejected, not cleaned. The direction is a ternary over two fixed strings — never the raw input, not even after checking it.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**Parameterize values. Allowlist identifiers.** There is no third technique, and "escape it carefully" is not a fourth.

The deeper point is that neither technique required you to decide what a dangerous character is. That decision is where defences go wrong, and both of these remove the need to make it.

workedExamples.title: Making a user-supplied link safe
workedExamples.problem:
Organisers can add a "tickets" link to their event page, rendered as `<a href="${url}">`. An organiser sets `url` to `javascript:fetch('/api/transfer',{method:'POST'})`. A fan clicks it, and their session performs a transfer.

Work out why the obvious defences fail, then build one that works.
steps: **Check whether HTML-escaping helps.** It does not, and this is the moment worth pausing on: the payload contains no angle brackets and no quotes. Every character in it survives an HTML encoder unchanged. A team that 'handles XSS' with output encoding alone is fully exposed here.

**Try a blocklist, and watch it fail.** Blocking the literal string `javascript:` is defeated by `JaVaScRiPt:` (case), by `java\tscript:` (embedded control characters, which browsers strip), by leading whitespace, and by switching payloads entirely to `data:text/html;base64,…`. Each bypass invites another rule, and the ruleset never finishes.

**Note why parsing beats matching.** `new URL()` normalises case and strips the whitespace and control characters that defeated the blocklist, so the bypasses are handled by the parser rather than by rules you had to think of. You compare against `u.protocol`, which is already canonical.

**Choose the failure value deliberately.** Returning `"#"` means a bad link renders as a dead link. Throwing would invite a `try/catch` somewhere upstream that silently swallows the problem — and a swallowed security error fails open, exactly as in the review exercise.
workedExamples.conclusion:
Allowlist beats blocklist; structured parsing beats string matching; and a harmless failure value beats an exception someone will suppress.

This is the third appearance of the same principle — `ORDER BY` columns, CORS origins, URL schemes. Whenever the safe set is small and enumerable, enumerate it and refuse everything else.

givenSteps: **Given — the untrusted input.** `originalname` comes from the upload request. It is attacker-controlled in exactly the way a form field is, even though nobody typed it into a visible box — which is the 'only form fields are untrusted' misconception in its most common disguise.

**Given — the interpreter.** The filesystem path resolver is the interpreter here, and `/var/uploads/` plus the name is the flat string that mixes your instruction (the directory) with their data (the name).
blankedStepPrompts: Give the concrete attack against this code, with an example filename, and say what an attacker achieves. Then explain why a check like `if (name.includes("..")) reject()` is the wrong shape of fix — and what the right shape is.

The stored name is later echoed back and rendered in the organiser's dashboard and in a `Content-Disposition` download header. Name the two *additional* sinks that creates and what each needs — and state the general rule this illustrates.
blankedStepAnswers:
**The attack:** `originalname` of `../../etc/cron.d/evil` escapes the upload directory and writes an attacker-controlled file to an arbitrary path — path traversal, which here escalates to remote code execution. A filename of `../../../var/www/app/index.js` overwrites application code directly.

**Why the `..` check is the wrong shape:** it is a blocklist. It invites bypasses (`....//`, URL-encoded `%2e%2e`, absolute paths that ignore the prefix entirely, Windows separators) and requires you to predict every encoding.

**The right shape** is the same as everywhere else in this section: do not use the attacker's string in the instruction channel at all. Generate the stored filename yourself — a UUID plus an extension validated against an allowlist of permitted types — and keep the original name as *data* in a database column, never as part of a path. Then resolve the final path and assert it is still inside the upload directory as a defence-in-depth check.

**The two additional sinks:** the dashboard renders it as HTML, so it needs context-correct **output encoding** at render time; and the `Content-Disposition` header is its own parsing context, where quotes, semicolons, newlines and non-ASCII characters allow header injection or response splitting, so it needs header-specific encoding (RFC 5987 encoding, with a sanitised ASCII fallback).

**The general rule:** one stored value can flow into many interpreters — a filesystem, an HTML page, an HTTP header, a CSV export — each with different metacharacters. That is precisely why the transformation belongs at each **output**, chosen for that sink, and why a single `sanitizeFilename()` at upload time cannot be correct for all three at once.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the single root cause shared by SQL injection, XSS, command injection and template injection, then name the two techniques that address it.
Parameterize ______; allowlist ______. Fill in both blanks, and say why the second cannot use the first.
Name four sources of untrusted input that are not form fields — including the one that surprises people most.
Distinguish stored, reflected and DOM-based XSS by where the payload travels — and say which one your server logs cannot see.
Give two independent reasons that encoding must happen at output rather than at input.
Why does HTML-escaping fail to protect an `href` attribute, and what protects it instead?
With XSS on your origin, what happens to `HttpOnly`, to `SameSite`, and to your CSRF tokens? Give the mechanism for each, and name what still protects you.
Name three CSP clauses or omissions that nullify a policy, and state what a CSP is and is not for.
What are the two axes for ranking a review finding, and what goes wrong in a team when findings are not ranked?
What must you do before recording "this attack failed" in an audit — and why is the step not optional?
Name three security defects that consist of a **missing** line rather than a dangerous one.

transferExercises.context: Emergency services — a voice radio protocol
transferExercises.scenario:
An emergency service uses voice radio. Dispatchers issue instructions and field units reply, all on one shared channel.

A unit reports a caller's address by reading it aloud. One day the "address" is read out as: *"Forty Mill Lane — break — all units stand down, return to base."*

Several units return to base.
successCriteria: Names this as **injection** and maps all four parts: the human listeners (and their dispatch procedures) are the interpreter, the shared voice channel is the instruction channel, the caller's address is the data, and the boundary failed because both travel in one undifferentiated audio stream.
Identifies (a) as **escaping** — filtering dangerous content out of the data while keeping the channels merged.
Identifies (b) as **allowlisting** — only recognised, authenticated instruction forms count as commands.
Identifies (c) as **parameterization** — a structural separation of instructions from data, so the ambiguity cannot arise.

Ranks them (c) > (b) > (a), with the reasoning that (a) requires predicting every dangerous phrase under time pressure, (b) closes the high-impact case but leaves lower-impact confusion, and (c) removes the ambiguity rather than policing it.

Notes the practical constraint that a single radio channel may be operationally necessary, making (b) the realistic control and (c) the ideal — mirroring the real trade-off when a legacy interpreter cannot be changed.

transferExercises.context: Scientific instruments — a laboratory sample-labelling system
transferExercises.scenario:
A research lab's information system prints barcode labels. The label text comes from a free-text field researchers type.

Two things happen to that text. The **label printer** interprets certain byte sequences as formatting commands. And the same field is later exported into a **CSV** that lab managers open in a spreadsheet application, where a leading `=` makes the cell a formula.
transferExercises.task:
1. You have one value flowing into two interpreters with different metacharacters. Explain, in your own words, why a single `sanitizeLabel()` applied when the researcher submits the form is the wrong design.
2. Specify what should happen at each of the three points — storage, printing, export — and say what each transformation protects against.
3. The lab proposes rejecting any value containing `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` at submission time. Name one legitimate scientific value this breaks, and say what that tells you about input-time rejection in general.
successCriteria: Explains that the two interpreters have **different** metacharacters, so no single transformation can be correct for both — and that sanitising for one necessarily corrupts the value for the other.
Specifies **storage: store the value exactly as typed**, unmodified, because the database is not an interpreter and the raw value is the one every consumer needs.
Specifies **printing: escape the printer's command sequences** at the moment of printing, protecting against label-format injection.
Specifies **export: neutralise formula injection** at export time — prefix with an apostrophe or quote the field — protecting against CSV formula execution in the spreadsheet application.
Names a legitimate broken value such as `pH=7.4`, `-80C storage`, `+/- 0.5mg`, or an email address in a contact field.

Draws the general conclusion that input-time rejection **destroys legitimate data to protect a specific downstream interpreter**, and that the correct layer is each output, where the destination and therefore the rules are actually known.

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this matters

This is the convergence point of the whole course. The audit cannot be completed without exercising every competency in it, which is exactly what makes it the transfer check for all of them at once.

It is also the only part that tells you something you do not already believe. Everything up to here has been you agreeing with a course. This is your application disagreeing with you — or failing to, for reasons you are now required to confirm rather than assume.

contentBlocks.title: Scope — read before you start
contentBlocks.content:
**Your own application only.** Your own local or staging environment only.

Write the sentence "In scope: …" at the top of your document before you run a single request, and keep to it. Attacking systems you do not own is illegal in most jurisdictions regardless of intent, and "I was doing a course exercise" is not a defence.

If your staging environment shares a database or an identity provider with production, it is not in scope until that is untangled.

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Attack the application you built across all three sections, from an explicit checklist, confirming the mechanism behind every result — then produce a ranked, honest audit document.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: Your own project app, on your own local or staging environment. Nothing else, ever.
instructions: **Set scope in writing first.** Write "In scope: …" before you start, and keep to it.
**Work the five-item checklist in order, without improvising.** The checklist exists precisely because your improvisation is shaped by the design already in your head.
Steal a session: copy the cookie to another browser, test logout in one browser against the copy in the other, and test whether a pre-login identifier survives authentication.
Forge a request: use the HTML page from the previous lab. Try POST, and if any state-changing GET exists, try an `` tag.

Inject payloads: `' OR '1'='1` and `'; SELECT 1 --` into every text field, filter, sort parameter and logged header; then `` into every field that renders anywhere — including admin dashboards, CSV exports and emails.
Bypass authorization: as a low-privilege user, change every id in every URL, call admin endpoints directly, and send fields the UI does not show, such as `{"role": "admin"}` in a profile update.
Abuse the edges: a filename of `../../etc/passwd`, a 10 MB display name, `null`/`[]`/`{}` where a string is expected, and a password-reset token replayed twice.

**Confirm every mechanism.** For each attack that *failed*, temporarily disable the control you believe stopped it, confirm the attack then succeeds, and re-enable it. Record both results. An entry without this step is incomplete.
**Rank what you found** by exploitability × blast radius.
**Fix, then re-test** — including one re-test of an attack that already failed, to confirm your fix did not disable an earlier control.
Write the residual-risk section. "None" is not a credible answer: every system has residual risk, and naming it is what distinguishes an audit from a reassurance.
materialsOrPrerequisites: Your project app with both previous labs completed, on local or staging.
Two browsers or one plus a private window, for the session-copying tests.
`curl` or an HTTP client that lets you set headers and bodies freely.
The forged-request HTML page you wrote in the previous lab.
reflectionPrompts: How many of your attack attempts came from the checklist rather than from your own intuition? What does that ratio suggest about auditing your own work unaided?
Which failed attack turned out to be stopped by a *different* control than the one you assumed? That gap is the value of the confirm-the-mechanism step.
Which of this course's misconceptions did you personally hold before starting, and what specifically changed your mind?
What is in your residual-risk section — and would you be comfortable reading it aloud to the person who owns this system?

selfAssessmentCriteria: My document opens with an explicit scope statement written before I started testing.
Every attack attempt has a row: attack, exact payload or steps, result, control responsible, how that control was confirmed, fix, residual risk.
Every "attack failed" row names how the mechanism was confirmed — not what I assumed stopped it.
Findings are ranked by exploitability and blast radius, not listed flat.
I re-tested at least one previously-failing attack after making fixes, to check I did not disable an earlier control.
My residual-risk section is non-empty and specific.
I wrote the paragraph naming a misconception I personally held and what changed my mind.

retrievalPractice.prompt: List the six fields every row of an audit table needs, and say which one distinguishes a finding from a guess.
Why must a self-audit work from a checklist you did not derive from your own design?

transferExercises.context: Food safety — a restaurant kitchen self-inspection
transferExercises.scenario: A head chef inspects their own kitchen the day before an unannounced food-safety visit. They walk through, see nothing wrong, and record "all clear". The inspector arrives and finds three violations within twenty minutes — none of them hidden, all of them in plain sight.
transferExercises.task:
Explain what happened using this section's reasoning about auditing your own work, without using any software vocabulary.

Then design a self-inspection procedure for the chef that would have caught at least two of the three violations, and identify which element of your procedure corresponds to "confirm the mechanism" — the step that distinguishes checking from assuming.
successCriteria: Explains that the chef inspected the kitchen they **imagined** — the routines they designed and therefore cannot see past — while the inspector tested paths the chef never considered.
Recognises that familiarity is the obstacle, not carelessness, and that this cannot be fixed by trying harder.
Designs a procedure using an **external, explicit checklist** rather than a walkthrough, so the list supplies the ideas the chef's intuition does not.

Includes at least one element that forces a change of perspective — inspecting in a different order, having a different person walk it, or checking against the written standard rather than from memory.

Identifies the confirm-the-mechanism analogue: **testing the control rather than observing the outcome** — e.g. checking that the fridge thermometer is accurate and that the alarm actually fires, rather than noting that the temperature reads correctly today.
Avoids all software vocabulary while keeping the structure of the argument intact.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** a salt must be kept secret for password hashing to be effective.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Salts are stored in plaintext beside the hash and must be readable to verify a login at all. Their purpose is to defeat precomputation and cross-user reuse, not to hide anything.
Correct. A salt is public by design. The secrecy that matters belongs to the password; the salt's job is to make each hash unique.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Are salts secret? What is a salt actually for?

errorPatterns.description: Treats the salt as a secret, often proposing a single global pepper stored separately in place of per-user salts.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read the *Storing a password you must never learn* section and trace which verification step becomes impossible if the salt cannot be read.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** rotating the session identifier at login prevents session fixation.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Fixation requires the attacker's pre-login identifier to survive authentication; issuing a new one and destroying the old removes that condition.
Rotation is precisely the defence against fixation. You may be thinking of session *theft* after login, which rotation does not address — that is what revocation is for.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Which attack does rotating the session identifier at login prevent, and how does that attack work?

errorPatterns.description: Confuses session fixation with post-login session theft, and concludes rotation does not help.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read the session fixation walkthrough and identify the exact moment at which the attacker's identifier would have to be invalidated.

questions.prompt: You inherit a service storing passwords as `sha256(salt + password)` with a unique 16-byte random salt per user. Which statement is accurate?
options: This is adequate; the per-user salt defeats precomputation, which is the main threat.
The salt defeats precomputation, but SHA-256's speed still allows fast offline brute-forcing of individual rows; a memory-hard hash is needed.
It is insecure because the salt is stored in plaintext; salts belong in a separate secrets manager.
It is secure provided the salt is at least 32 bytes and the database is encrypted at rest.

optionFeedback.feedback: It defeats precomputation only. Each row can still be brute-forced individually at GPU speed, because the hash is fast by design.
Correct — and the value of this answer is that it separates the two attacks and names the one still unaddressed.
Salts are not secrets and never were; they must be readable to verify a login.
Neither salt length nor encryption at rest addresses speed, and an attacker with a database dump has decrypted data by definition.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Passwords stored as a fast hash plus a per-user salt: which attack is defeated, and which remains?

errorPatterns.description: Treats salting as a complete solution, not recognising that hash speed is an independent vulnerability.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Revisit the two-attacks breakdown and the runnable salting example, then compare a fast hash's guess rate against a tuned work factor.

questions.prompt: Your session cookie is `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`. An attacker achieves stored XSS on your site. What have you actually prevented?
options: Nothing — HttpOnly is ineffective once script runs in your origin.
The attacker cannot act as the user, because the cookie is unreadable.
Theft of the identifier, but not the attacker issuing authenticated requests from within the page.
Both theft and use, because SameSite=Lax also blocks the injected script's requests.

optionFeedback.feedback: An overcorrection. HttpOnly genuinely does stop `document.cookie` from reading the identifier, which blocks exfiltration.
Unreadable is not unusable — the browser attaches the cookie to requests the injected script makes.
Correct. This is exactly the boundary: HttpOnly stops reading, not acting.
The injected script runs on your origin, so its requests are same-site and SameSite has no opinion about them.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: HttpOnly prevents ___ but not ___. Which of the two does an attacker usually need?

errorPatterns.description: Believes HttpOnly makes XSS survivable by preventing the attacker from acting as the user.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read the cookie attribute table, paying attention to the right-hand column, and re-run the section-three XSS impact question.

questions.prompt: A login endpoint returns the identical message and status code for both failure modes, but returns immediately when no account exists. A colleague says enumeration is closed. Are they right?
options: Yes — identical message and status means an attacker cannot distinguish the two cases.
No — the response duration still distinguishes them, because only the existing-user path pays for the hash.
Yes, provided the endpoint is also rate-limited per IP address.
No — but only because the HTTP response body length will differ between the two cases.

optionFeedback.feedback: Matching text and status closes two channels of three. The timing gap between a 0.1 ms miss and a 200 ms hash is a clean, scriptable oracle.
Correct. Hash unconditionally against a dummy salt so both paths cost the same.
Rate limiting raises the cost of bulk enumeration, which is worthwhile, but it does not remove the signal — and a patient attacker is still an attacker.
The premise says the messages are identical, so the bodies are the same length. The real leak is duration.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Identical message, identical status, immediate return when no user exists. Is enumeration closed?

errorPatterns.description: Equalises the visible channels only, leaving a timing side channel that distinguishes existing from absent accounts.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the constant-time login challenge and re-read the worked example's step 3, then measure the two medians in your own app.

questions.prompt:
Design question. Your team ships a "log out everywhere" feature. The current logout handler calls `res.clearCookie("sid")` and returns 200.

Explain what has to change and why, then describe how you would **prove** the new feature works. Be specific about what evidence would convince a skeptical reviewer.
successCriteria: Identifies that logout must delete server-side session state, and that the current handler deletes nothing.
Explains that "log out everywhere" requires deleting *all* sessions for that user, which requires sessions to be queryable by user id.
Proposes concrete proof: capture an identifier, trigger the feature, replay the captured identifier and observe rejection.
Notes that the proof must use a copy taken *before* logout, from outside the browser that logged out.

rubric.excellent: Identifies the server-side delete as the core change, explains that sessions must be indexed by user id for the "everywhere" variant, and proposes proof using an identifier captured beforehand and replayed from outside the browser — ideally noting that any stateless token component has its own revocation problem that a session delete does not solve.
rubric.adequate: Says logout must delete the server-side session and proposes replaying a copied identifier as proof, but does not address how *all* sessions are found, or proposes proof that only tests the logged-out browser.
rubric.weak: Describes clearing cookies more thoroughly, or proposes proof that consists of checking the user appears logged out in their own browser — which is exactly the evidence the broken implementation also produces.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: "Log out everywhere" on top of a cookie-clearing logout: what must change, and how would you prove it works?

errorPatterns.description: Treats logout as a browser-side operation and proposes proof that only observes the browser that initiated it.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-run the predict-then-run logout snippet, then repeat the lab step that replays a copied identifier with curl after logging out.

errorPatterns.description: Assumes the cookie's contents being signed or 'encrypted' means the session cannot be reused once the browser discards it.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read the misconception callout distinguishing signing from encryption, and note that possession, not disclosure, is the threat.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** because a JWT is signed, its contents cannot be read without the signing key.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Signing provides integrity, not confidentiality. The payload is base64url-encoded and readable by anyone holding the token.
Correct. Encoding is not encryption — never put anything in a JWT you would not print on the outside of an envelope.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Can a JWT's claims be read without the signing key?

errorPatterns.description: Treats a signed token's payload as confidential and places sensitive data in claims.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-run the runnable example that decodes a token payload with no key, and audit your own tokens for anything you would not print publicly.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** stateless tokens can be revoked instantly without the server consulting any stored state.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Revocation is inherently a change of server-side mind about an already-issued credential, which requires state — a denylist, a version counter, or short expiry plus a stateful refresh token.
Correct. Statelessness and instant revocation are in direct tension; every real deployment reintroduces state somewhere.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Can a stateless token be revoked instantly with no server-side state?

errorPatterns.description: Assumes revocation works in a stateless design without identifying the mechanism that would make it work.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the 60-second revocation worked example and name the property abandoned at step 4.

options: Claims might be stale if the user's role changed after the token was issued.
The payload is readable by the client, exposing the role.
No signature verification occurs, so anyone can mint a token claiming role: "admin".
The token could be replayed from another service that shares the signing key.

optionFeedback.feedback: True and worth fixing, but far less severe: staleness requires a legitimately issued token, while forgery requires nothing at all.
Also true and inherent to JWTs, but disclosure is not the severe problem here.
Correct. `decode` parses without verifying, so every claim it returns is attacker-supplied.
A real audience-confusion risk, but it presupposes verification is happening at all — and here it is not.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Code reads a role claim straight from `jwt.decode(token)`. What is the worst consequence?

errorPatterns.description: Treats decoding as validation and reads claims before any signature check.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the validator challenge and note where the signature check sits relative to every claim read.

questions.prompt: Your validator selects its verification algorithm from the token's own `alg` header. An attacker who has your **public** key — which is public — can now do what?
options: Nothing, as long as your private key remains secret.
Read the payload of any token, but not create one.
Send alg: none to bypass verification, or downgrade RS256 to HS256 and sign with your public key as the shared secret.
Only replay tokens they have already captured, within their expiry window.

optionFeedback.feedback: The private key stays secret and is no longer required. The attacker changes which algorithm you use, and your validator obeys.
Reading the payload requires no key at all, and is not what this defect enables.
Correct — both attacks, and both come from the same root cause: the token told your validator how to check it.
Replay is possible against any bearer token; this defect enables outright forgery, which is strictly worse.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A validator picks its algorithm from the token's `alg` header. Name the two attacks this enables.

errorPatterns.description: Selects the verification algorithm from attacker-controlled data rather than from configuration.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read step 2 of the validation order and confirm your own validator takes the algorithm from an explicit allowlist in configuration.

questions.prompt:
Design question. Your mobile app uses stateless access tokens. Compliance now requires that a suspended employee loses access **within 60 seconds**.

Describe your design, and state explicitly what property you gave up to meet the requirement. Then name one operational risk your design introduces that the previous stateless design did not have.
successCriteria: Proposes short-lived access tokens plus a server-stored, rotating refresh token.
Recognises that short expiry alone cannot meet a 60-second deadline, and adds a revocation check (a `jti` denylist) on the request path.
States plainly that **statelessness** was the property given up.
Names a concrete operational risk — a new hot-path dependency, and the fail-open/fail-closed decision when it is unavailable.
Optionally notes that refresh-token rotation provides theft detection a stateless design cannot.

rubric.excellent: Proposes short access tokens with rotating server-side refresh tokens, correctly identifies that meeting a 60-second deadline requires a revocation lookup on the request path, states that statelessness was the trade, and names the denylist as a new tier-one hot-path dependency with an explicit fail-closed decision. Notes that rotation gives theft detection as a bonus.
rubric.adequate: Proposes short-lived tokens plus refresh tokens and acknowledges some server state is needed, but is vague about how the 60-second deadline is actually met, or names the trade without identifying an operational risk.
rubric.weak: Proposes shortening token lifetimes alone, or asserts revocation works without describing a mechanism — which is the misconception that statelessness costs nothing.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Stateless tokens, but suspension must take effect within 60 seconds. What is your design, and what did you give up?

errorPatterns.description: Claims a stateless design meets a hard revocation deadline without adding any server-side lookup.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Rework the refresh/revocation worked example and identify the exact step at which state is reintroduced.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** role checks can safely live in route middleware, but ownership checks generally cannot.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Role checks need only the identity, which middleware has. Ownership checks need the loaded record, which middleware does not yet have.
Consider the request lifecycle: at the moment route middleware runs, has the record been fetched yet? If not, what would the ownership check compare against?

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Which authorization check belongs in middleware and which cannot, and why?

errorPatterns.description: Attempts to enforce object-level rules in route middleware, producing either no check or a duplicate query that drifts.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read *Where enforcement has to live* and mark the exact line at which the record first exists.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** a correctly configured CORS policy prevents attackers from calling your API from a script.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: CORS is enforced by browsers on responses. curl, servers and mobile apps ignore it entirely, and even in a browser a simple request is delivered and executed.
Correct. CORS protects users' browsers from reading cross-origin responses. It provides your API no protection at all.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Does a restrictive CORS policy stop an attacker calling your API from a script?

errorPatterns.description: Relies on CORS as an access-control mechanism for the API rather than as a browser read-restriction.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Call your own CORS-restricted endpoint with curl and observe the normal successful response.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** CSRF requires the attacker to obtain a copy of the victim's session cookie.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: The defining property is the opposite: the attacker never holds the credential. The browser attaches it automatically, which is what makes it a confused-deputy attack.
Correct. The attacker causes the request and never sees the cookie or the response — the effect is the goal.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Does a CSRF attacker need a copy of the victim's session cookie?

errorPatterns.description: Models CSRF as credential theft rather than as abuse of ambient authority.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read the confused-deputy explanation and note that the attacker never reads the response.

questions.prompt: `GET /api/submissions/:id` calls `requireLogin`, then `requireRole("teacher")`, then returns the record. A teacher reads a submission from a class she does not teach. What failed?
options: Authentication — her session should not have been valid for that resource.
Nothing; teachers are trusted staff and role-level access is the intended design.
Object-level authorization — the role was checked but the relationship between this teacher and this record was not.
CORS — the API should have rejected the cross-origin request.

optionFeedback.feedback: Her session is valid and her identity is correct. Nothing about authentication failed.
This is over-permissioning by policy, and it is how one compromised teacher account exposes an entire district.
Correct — classic IDOR/BOLA. Right kind of user, wrong record.
CORS governs browser reads across origins and has no bearing on which records a user may access.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A handler checks login and role, then returns a record by id. A teacher reads another class's submission. What failed?

errorPatterns.description: Accepts a role check as sufficient authorization, omitting the ownership or relationship comparison.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the policy-function challenge, focusing on the two cases that differ only in `classIds`.

errorPatterns.description: Argues the defect is unreachable because the interface never offers the action.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Repeat the lab step that curls the endpoint whose button the UI hides, using a valid low-privilege session.

questions.prompt: Your API allows only `https://app.schools.test`. A page on `https://evil.test` sends a cross-origin POST with a form-encoded body and `credentials: "include"`. The console shows a CORS error. What happened on the server?
options: Nothing — the browser blocked the request before it was sent.
The request was delivered and the handler executed; only the response was withheld from the page.
The request was sent but arrived without cookies, so it ran unauthenticated.
The server rejected it because the Origin header was not allowlisted.

optionFeedback.feedback: True of preflighted requests. A form-encoded POST is a *simple* request — it was sent, and it ran.
Correct, and this is precisely why CORS is not a defence for state-changing endpoints.
This conflates CORS with SameSite; whether cookies attach is decided by the cookie's own attributes.
Unless you wrote an explicit server-side Origin check, your server does not reject based on Origin — it omits a response header.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A cross-origin POST produces a CORS error in the console. What already happened on the server?

errorPatterns.description: Believes a CORS error means the request never reached the server, and therefore that CORS protects mutating endpoints.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Repeat the lab step that sends a cross-origin POST under a restrictive config and then checks the database for the write.

questions.prompt: A JSON-only API uses session cookies with `SameSite=Lax`, requires `Content-Type: application/json`, and allows only its own frontend origin via CORS. Which statement best describes its CSRF exposure?
options: None — SameSite=Lax eliminates CSRF.
None — CORS restricts which origins may call the API.
Substantially reduced, with residual exposure via state-changing GET endpoints, same-site subdomains, and any endpoint that also accepts form-encoded bodies.
Unchanged — only a synchroniser token provides any CSRF protection at all.

optionFeedback.feedback: State-changing GETs and same-site subdomains both bypass Lax.
CORS does not prevent requests being sent; it governs response reading.
Correct. Each layer is real, each has a named gap, and this option names them.
This dismisses genuine layers — SameSite and the JSON content-type preflight requirement both materially reduce exposure.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: SameSite=Lax, JSON-only, restrictive CORS. What CSRF exposure remains?

errorPatterns.description: Treats SameSite=Lax as a complete CSRF solution and stops layering.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the cookie-attachment challenge, focusing on the top-level GET and subdomain cases.

errorPatterns.description: Assumes an API design is CSRF-immune without auditing for cookie-carrying paths.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Inventory every path in your app that authenticates via a cookie rather than an explicit header.

successCriteria: States that reflecting the Origin with credentials grants **every origin on the internet** credentialed read access to the API.
Explains that any page the victim visits can then read API responses as that victim.
Notes that the wildcard cannot be combined with credentials, which is why teams reach for reflection in the first place.
Gives the correct configuration: an exact-match allowlist of enumerated origins, explicit methods and headers, credentials only where needed.
Identifies a commonly forgotten detail — `Vary: Origin` (cache poisoning across origins) or gating localhost on non-production — and says what breaks without it.

rubric.excellent: Explains that reflection plus credentials is strictly worse than the wildcard because it grants cross-origin *account* access to any site the victim visits; correctly notes the wildcard/credentials incompatibility as the motivation; specifies an exact-match allowlist with enumerated methods and headers; and names `Vary: Origin` with the specific CDN cache-poisoning failure, or the localhost entry with the local-port attack path.
rubric.adequate: Identifies that reflection is dangerous and proposes an allowlist, but is vague about the scope of what is granted, or names a forgotten detail without saying what actually breaks.
rubric.weak: Proposes suffix or regex matching on the origin, or treats the wildcard as an acceptable alternative for a credentialed API — both of which preserve the vulnerability in a different shape.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Reflecting the Origin header while allowing credentials: what does it grant, to whom, and what is the correct configuration?

errorPatterns.description: Reflects the request Origin with credentials enabled, or matches origins by suffix/regex rather than exact equality.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the CORS responder challenge, particularly the `evil-app.schools.test` lookalike case, and re-read the configuration worked example.

questions.prompt:
Harden `POST /api/orders/:id/cancel` against CSRF.

List the layers you would apply in order. For **each** one, state the specific attack it stops and the specific attack it does not. Finish with the sentence that belongs in your audit notes beginning "If an attacker achieves XSS on this origin…".
successCriteria: Confirms the endpoint is not reachable by GET, and says why that matters.
Applies `SameSite=Lax` and names its two gaps: top-level GET navigation and same-site subdomains.
Adds a session-bound synchroniser token in a custom header, compared in constant time, and names XSS as its defeat condition.
Adds an Origin check as defence-in-depth, noting Referer's unreliability and the absent-header decision.
Keeps the authorization check independent, and explains that a forged request from an unprivileged user's browser fails there regardless.
Ends with an explicit residual-risk sentence naming which layers fail simultaneously under XSS.

rubric.excellent: Gives all five layers in a sensible order with a specific stop/does-not-stop pair for each; treats authorization as orthogonal rather than as another CSRF layer; and writes a residual-risk sentence identifying that SameSite, the token and the Origin check all fail together under XSS, leaving authorization and re-authentication.
rubric.adequate: Lists the main layers and gets most gaps right, but treats one layer as complete, or omits the authorization layer, or writes a vague residual-risk sentence that does not name which layers fail together.
rubric.weak: Proposes a single control as sufficient — usually SameSite or a token alone — or offers no residual-risk statement, which is the belief this section exists to correct.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Harden a state-changing POST against CSRF in layers. For each layer: what it stops, what it does not.

errorPatterns.description: Treats a CSRF token as protective against XSS, or omits the residual-risk statement entirely.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-open the CSRF defence-stack playground, set `hasXss` to true, and observe which layers collapse together.

errorPatterns.description: Relies on a Referer or Origin check as the primary CSRF control.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Log Origin and Referer presence across real traffic for a day before proposing either as a control.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** using an ORM eliminates SQL injection risk.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: ORMs parameterize the queries they generate, but raw-query escape hatches, dynamic column names and string-built where clauses all bypass that protection.
Correct. Grep your codebase for `raw`, `literal`, `whereRaw` and `queryRawUnsafe` before believing you are covered.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Does using an ORM eliminate SQL injection risk?

errorPatterns.description: Assumes ORM usage is a blanket guarantee and does not audit raw-query escape hatches.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Grep the project for the ORM's raw-query methods and review each call site individually.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** a value read back out of your own database can safely be treated as trusted.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: If an attacker wrote it earlier, it is attacker-controlled data that merely took a detour through storage — exactly how stored XSS and second-order injection work.
Correct. Untrusted means *not computed by you*, regardless of how many systems the value has passed through since.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Is a value read back out of your own database trusted?

errorPatterns.description: Validates input once at the boundary and treats stored values as safe forever after.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the untrusted-inputs exercise and list every field of a request object as computed-by-us or influenced-by-someone-else.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** HTML-escaping a value is sufficient before placing it inside an `href` attribute.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: `javascript:alert(1)` contains no HTML metacharacters at all, so an HTML encoder passes it through unchanged. URL contexts need parsing and a scheme allowlist.
Correct. Parse the URL and allowlist the scheme — the same allowlist principle as `ORDER BY` columns and CORS origins.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Is HTML-escaping enough before putting a value in an `href`?

errorPatterns.description: Applies one escaping routine to all contexts, leaving URL and script contexts unprotected.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the safeUrl challenge and compare its approach with the context-aware encoder.

questions.prompt: A handler builds `ORDER BY ${req.query.sort}`. Which fix is correct?
options: Escape the value with the driver's string-escaping function before interpolating.
Pass it as a bound parameter: ORDER BY ?.
Map the input through an allowlist of permitted column names and reject anything unmatched.
Strip all non-alphanumeric characters from the input, then interpolate.

optionFeedback.feedback: Escaping applies to string literals. A column name is an identifier, so escaping either breaks the query or leaves it injectable.
Placeholders bind values; `ORDER BY ?` sorts by a constant and does not do what the developer intends.
Correct. The interpolated text then originates from your code, not from the user's input.
Reduces the surface without closing it — `ORDER BY` targets can still be abused for blind extraction — and it is the escaping-instead-of-separating pattern again.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: A user picks the SQL sort column. Parameterization cannot bind it. What is the correct technique?

errorPatterns.description: Attempts to make a user-supplied identifier safe by escaping or filtering it rather than allowlisting.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Rework the ORDER BY worked example and note why step 3 rejects escaping outright.

questions.prompt: Your team proposes HTML-escaping all user input at the API boundary before storing it. What is the strongest objection?
options: It is too slow to escape on every write.
The correct encoding depends on the output context, which is not known at input time — and pre-escaping corrupts the value for non-HTML consumers.
It works for HTML, but a Content-Security-Policy is a better substitute.
It is unnecessary because modern frameworks auto-escape everything.

optionFeedback.feedback: Performance is negligible and irrelevant to the correctness problem.
Correct — two independent arguments at once: contexts differ and are unknowable in advance, and stored data serves more consumers than the web page.
CSP mitigates damage but does not replace encoding, and the objection stands whether or not a CSP exists.
Auto-escaping has named escape hatches — raw-HTML props, URL attributes, inline script blocks.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why is escaping all user input at the API boundary the wrong layer? Give the strongest objection.

errorPatterns.description: Relies on framework auto-escaping without auditing its escape hatches.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Grep the codebase for `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `v-html` and URL-attribute interpolation, and review each occurrence.

questions.prompt: An attacker achieves stored XSS on a site using `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` session cookies and per-request CSRF tokens. What is the realistic impact?
options: Minimal — the cookie cannot be read and SameSite=Strict blocks the forged requests.
Limited to defacement, since the attacker cannot authenticate as the user.
Full compromise within the origin — the script reads CSRF tokens from the DOM and performs authenticated actions, even though it cannot read the cookie.
Serious only if the CSRF token is stored in localStorage rather than in the DOM.

optionFeedback.feedback: The injected script runs on your origin, so its requests are same-site and carry the cookie.
No authentication is needed — the requests are made by the user's own browser with the user's own session.
Correct. HttpOnly blocks exfiltration, not on-page action, and that distinction is the whole ranking of XSS severity.
The storage location is irrelevant; script in your origin reaches either one.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Stored XSS on a site with HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict and CSRF tokens. What is the realistic impact?

errorPatterns.description: Under-ranks XSS severity by assuming cookie protections constrain an attacker executing script in the origin.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read *What XSS costs*, then list which of your own defences survive script execution on your origin.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** a Content-Security-Policy containing `script-src 'unsafe-inline'` provides meaningful protection against injected scripts.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: Most XSS payloads are inline scripts or inline event handlers, which that directive explicitly permits — it largely nullifies the policy's anti-XSS value.
Correct. Use per-response nonces or hashes with `strict-dynamic`, plus `object-src 'none'` and `base-uri 'none'`.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Does a CSP with `script-src 'unsafe-inline'` meaningfully protect against injected scripts?

errorPatterns.description: Treats the presence of any CSP header as protection without evaluating its directives for bypasses.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read the CSP bypass list and evaluate your own policy against all six items.

questions.prompt:
A colleague says: "We've fixed SQL injection — we escape all quotes in user input before building queries."

Give the three strongest technical objections, each with a concrete example of an input or situation that defeats their approach. Then state what they should do instead, in one sentence.
successCriteria: Objection 1: **unquoted numeric parameters** need no quote at all — `WHERE id = 5 OR 1=1`.
Objection 2: **identifiers** (table names, column names, `ORDER BY` targets) are not string literals, so quoting cannot make them safe.
Objection 3: escaping is **charset-dependent** and historically bypassed via multi-byte encodings that construct a valid quote from escaped bytes.
States the alternative: parameterize values and allowlist identifiers.
Optionally notes that escaping also silently corrupts legitimate data such as names containing apostrophes.

rubric.excellent: Gives all three objections with concrete examples, correctly identifies that the identifier case cannot be solved by any escaping strategy at all, and states the two-technique alternative crisply. Ideally notes that the approach also breaks legitimate values like O'Brien, so it fails on correctness as well as security.
rubric.adequate: Gives two solid objections with examples and names parameterization as the alternative, but misses the identifier case or treats escaping as merely weaker rather than structurally wrong.
rubric.weak: Argues that escaping is insufficient without concrete examples, or proposes 'better escaping' or input filtering as the remedy — which is the same misconception restated.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: "We escape all quotes before building queries." Give three technical objections and the correct alternative.

errorPatterns.description: Proposes stronger escaping or input filtering rather than separating the instruction and data channels.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the safe-query challenge and observe where the injection payload ends up in a correct solution — intact in params, absent from sql.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** reviewing for security is primarily a matter of searching for dangerous functions like `eval` and `innerHTML`.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: That is a useful first pass, but most real defects are *missing* checks — absent ownership comparisons, unprotected routes, swallowed errors — and no search finds a line that was never written.
Correct. The reviewer's advantage over the scanner is the ability to ask *what should be here that isn't?*

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Is security review mainly about searching for dangerous function names?

errorPatterns.description: Reviews by scanning for dangerous identifiers and misses defects consisting of omissions.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo the admin refund review exercise and identify which defect no grep could have found.

questions.prompt: **True or false:** an exploit attempt that fails during a self-audit proves the corresponding defence is working.
options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: The failure may be incidental — a malformed payload, a framework default, a stripped header, a dev-mode difference. The mechanism must be confirmed.
Correct. Disable the suspected control, verify the attack then succeeds, and re-enable it. Only that identifies which line is doing the work.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Does a failed exploit attempt prove the corresponding defence works?

errorPatterns.description: Records a failed attack as evidence of a working control without confirming which control was responsible.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: For one failed attempt in your audit, disable the suspected control, confirm the attack succeeds, re-enable, and record both results.

options: A logging hygiene issue — the warning should be an error, but access control still functions.
A critical authorization bypass: the check throws, the catch swallows it, and execution continues to the refund.
A medium-severity issue, since only users who reach this route at all are affected.
No finding — wrapping authorization in try/catch is a standard defensive pattern.

optionFeedback.feedback: The log level is irrelevant. The defect is that a failed authorization check does not stop execution — the refund is issued either way.
Correct, and note the shape: the vulnerability is the *absence* of a return statement, which no scanner detects.
Severity depends on reachability, and this route has no authentication gate shown at all — so the affected population is everyone who can reach it.
Wrapping a control in a catch that logs and continues converts a security check into a log line. This is a fail-open pattern, not a defensive one.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: An authorization check is wrapped in a try/catch that logs and continues. What is the finding and its severity?

errorPatterns.description: Fails to recognise that catching and logging an authorization failure without returning permits the action.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read the *look for absences* list and audit your own catch blocks for swallowed security failures.

questions.prompt: You have four findings. Which should be ranked highest?
options: SQL injection in an admin-only report filter, reachable by three staff accounts.
An unauthenticated endpoint returning any user's order history by id.
A missing Vary: Origin header on a correctly allowlisted CORS response.
A session cookie missing the SameSite attribute on a JSON-only API that also requires a CSRF token.

optionFeedback.feedback: Catastrophic blast radius, but it requires an already-privileged account — so exploitability is materially lower than an unauthenticated defect. Ranking it first weights severity while ignoring reachability.
Correct: no barrier at all, and a blast radius of every user. Unauthenticated plus everyone's data is the worst square on the grid.
A real caching defect worth fixing, with no direct path to compromise given a correct allowlist.
Worth fixing, and materially mitigated by the remaining layers — this is what defence in depth is for.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Rank by exploitability and blast radius: which finding is highest priority, and why?

questions.prompt:

Follows each value to where it is **interpreted** — a query, a template, a shell, a page, a redirect, a file path.
Explicitly hunts **absences**: missing ownership checks, routes below the middleware line, swallowed authorization errors, roles added to an enum but not to the policy function.
Ranks findings by **exploitability** and **blast radius**, and is willing to mark something low.
Explains that scanners match patterns that exist, while most real defects are lines that were never written.

rubric.excellent: Gives a reproducible method — enumerate entry points, trace each value to its interpreter, check each trust boundary for a transformation, and separately hunt a named list of common absences — then ranks on both axes and explains the scanner gap precisely as a detection asymmetry between present patterns and missing lines. Mentions checking the policy function for completeness against the role enum.
rubric.adequate: Describes tracing input to sinks and looking for missing checks, and mentions prioritisation, but the method is loose or the scanner explanation is asserted rather than reasoned.
rubric.weak: Describes scanning for dangerous functions, or lists vulnerability categories to look for without a method for locating them in unfamiliar code.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Describe your method for reviewing an unfamiliar codebase for security defects in two hours.

errorPatterns.description: Lists vulnerability categories rather than a systematic method for finding them in unfamiliar code.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-read *Reviewing code you did not write* and apply the entry-point-to-sink trace to one file of your own project.

questions.prompt:
Write the audit entry for one attack you attempted against your own application that **failed**.

Include every field a complete entry needs. Then explain, in one or two sentences, why an entry reading "tried CSRF, didn't work" would be worthless to the person who reads this document in six months.

Names the **control responsible** and states **how that was confirmed** — by disabling it and observing the attack succeed.
Notes the fix (or that none was needed) and the residual risk.
Explains that an unconfirmed entry does not identify which control did the work, so a future refactor can remove the real protection while the audit still reads 'not exploitable'.
Demonstrates the confirm-the-mechanism discipline rather than merely describing it.

rubric.excellent: A complete, concrete entry with all six fields, where the confirmation step names the specific control disabled and the observed change in outcome. The explanation identifies the precise failure mode of unconfirmed entries: they record an outcome rather than a cause, so nobody can tell later which line of code was load-bearing.
rubric.adequate: Includes most fields and mentions confirming the mechanism, but the confirmation is described generically, or the explanation of why it matters is thin.
rubric.weak: Records the attack and the outcome only, with no mechanism confirmation — which is exactly the entry the question asks the learner to critique.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Write a complete audit entry for an attack that failed, and say why "tried it, didn't work" is worthless.
