glossary.definition: A secret where possession alone proves identity. Whoever holds a session identifier *is* that user to your server — there is no second factor inside the string, which is why theft, revocation and rotation are the whole design problem.
A unique random value stored in plaintext beside each password hash. It defeats precomputation (rainbow tables) and cross-user reuse. It is **not** a secret and was never meant to be.

A hash function deliberately requiring a large block of RAM per guess (scrypt, Argon2). Memory is what GPUs and ASICs are short of, so memory-hardness — not just slowness — is what blunts mass cracking.
Comparing two secrets so that the time taken does not depend on where they first differ. `hmac.compare_digest` in Python, `crypto.timingSafeEqual` in Node. Ordinary `==` short-circuits and leaks.
Learning whether an account exists from a system's response. Leaks through three channels at once: the message text, the status code, and the response duration. All three must be equalised.

An attack where the attacker plants a session identifier on the victim before login; if the server keeps that identifier after authenticating, the attacker now holds an authenticated session. Defeated by rotating the identifier at every privilege change.

A cookie attribute hiding the value from `document.cookie`. It stops injected script from **reading** the session identifier. It does not stop injected script from **acting** as the user, because the browser still attaches the cookie.

A cookie attribute controlling whether the cookie rides cross-site requests. `Strict` withholds always; `Lax` allows top-level GET navigations; `None` opts out entirely and requires `Secure`. Subdomains are same-site, so it says nothing about them.

JSON Web Token: three base64url segments — header, payload, signature — where the signature covers the first two. The payload is encoded, not encrypted, so anyone holding the token can read every claim.
A named statement inside a token payload, such as `sub`, `exp`, `aud` or `iss`. Claims are only trustworthy after the signature has been verified — reading them first is the classic mistake.

A long-lived, server-stored credential exchanged for short-lived access tokens. Rotating it on each use gives you theft detection: the same refresh token presented twice means a copy exists, and the whole family can be revoked.
Establishing who is making a request. Its failure mode is someone being a user they are not, and its status code is 401.

Deciding whether the identified requester may perform this action on this resource. Its failure mode is a correctly identified user doing something they shouldn't, and its status code is 403 — or 404 where the record's existence is itself sensitive.

Insecure Direct Object Reference, also called BOLA: an endpoint loads a record by an identifier the caller supplied and never checks the record belongs to them. Consistently the most-reported API vulnerability in the field.

A policy function whose final statement returns false, so any action or resource type nobody wrote a rule for is refused rather than allowed. The opposite default turns every unanticipated case into a hole.

The browser rule that script on one origin may **send** a request to another origin but may not **read** the response without permission. That asymmetry — sending is allowed, reading is not — produces both CORS and CSRF.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: the protocol by which a server tells the browser to relax the same-origin policy for named origins. It is a relaxation mechanism protecting users' browsers, not a protection for your API — non-browser clients ignore it entirely.

An `OPTIONS` request a browser sends before non-simple cross-origin requests (JSON content types, custom headers, PUT/DELETE) to ask permission. Preflighted requests really are stopped before arrival; simple requests are not.

Authority applied automatically, without anyone deciding per request that it should be. A browser attaching cookies to every request aimed at your origin is ambient authority, and CSRF is its direct consequence.
Cross-Site Request Forgery: a hostile page causes the victim's browser to send an authenticated state-changing request. The attacker never holds or reads the credential — the effect is the goal.
The general pattern behind CSRF: a privileged party (the browser) is tricked by an unprivileged one (a hostile page) into exercising its authority on that party's behalf.

A random, session-bound value embedded in your own pages and required on state-changing requests. A cross-site attacker cannot read your page to obtain it — but script running inside your origin can, which is why XSS defeats it.

Cross-Site Scripting: attacker-supplied data is parsed as markup or script in your page. Stored, reflected and DOM-based variants differ only in where the payload travels. Its impact is total compromise of the origin.

An XSS whose payload never reaches the server: client-side JavaScript reads it from `location.hash`, `postMessage` or storage and writes it into a dangerous sink. Server-side defences and server logs are both blind to it.

A place where a value is interpreted rather than merely stored or displayed — `innerHTML`, `eval`, an `href`, a SQL string, a shell command line. Encoding is chosen by the sink's context, not by the value.

Transforming a value at the moment it is written into a specific context (HTML body, attribute, URL, script). It must happen at output because the correct transformation depends on a destination that is unknown at input time.
A response header restricting which script sources a browser will execute. It limits what an injection can do; it does not prevent the injection, and `'unsafe-inline'` largely nullifies it.

Attacker-controlled data crossing into an interpreter's instruction channel. SQL, HTML, shell, template and NoSQL injection are one bug in different clothes, with one structural fix: keep the channels separate.

A query whose text is parsed into a plan first, with placeholders in the value positions, and whose values are bound afterwards. A bound value can never become syntax, because parsing has already finished.
Accepting only members of a small enumerated safe set and rejecting everything else. The required tool wherever parameterization cannot reach — SQL identifiers, `ORDER BY` targets, URL schemes.
Anything you did not compute yourself: form fields, but also headers, cookies, filenames, webhook payloads, partner APIs, and rows an attacker wrote into your own database earlier.

How much is exposed when a defect is exploited — one record, one user, every user, or the whole system. Ranked together with exploitability, it is what turns a list of findings into an actionable review.

How reachable a defect is: by an unauthenticated stranger, by any logged-in user, or only by someone who already holds the privilege. Ignoring it is how a real bypass gets buried under theoretical findings.
